#1635. Pressure mounts on under-fire Regis Le Bris as Sunderland lose again, Bournemouth's super-subs preserve their flawless start, Pierre Sage is handed a Crystal Palace lifeline after late equaliser, while Brighton win

By MILES STARFORTH and LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and WILL PICKWORTH, SPORTS REPORTER and JAMES SHARPE

Published: 15:39 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:40 EST, 5 November 2026

Sunderland's unbeaten start to their first European campaign in 53 years was brought to an abrupt end by Dinamo Zagreb to pile more pressure on Regis Le Bris ahead of Chelsea's visit to Wearside.

The Croatian side won 2-0 to heap more misery on Le Bris and his team at the Stadium of Light following a dismal start to the season in which his team has won just one Premier League fixture.

There were Bonfire Night fireworks across Wearside, and before the game at the Stadium of Light, but not enough on the pitch from Sunderland, who only came to life after the break.

Europa League football has been an antidote to domestic doom and gloom for Sunderland fans, with the club having made a bright start to its first European campaign in 53 years by winning two and drawing one of their first three group phase fixtures.

But it was Dinamo who would light up the first half with two moments of quality from Luke Stojkovic and Dion Beljo.

Le Bris had labelled the season as 'probably the most demanding challenge Sunderland has faced in its history' before the game, which followed a 3-1 defeat by newly-promoted Coventry City. The 3-1 loss left the Carabao Cup quarter-finalists rooted to the bottom of the Premier League with just five points from nine games, and Le Bris under scrutiny ahead of a challenging run of fixtures.

Roger Le Bris is under increasing pressure at Sunderland after seeing his side lose once again

Granit Xhaka cuts a forlorn figure as Sunderland's unbeaten Europa League start ends

Le Bris, mindful of Sunday's Premier League game against fourth-placed Chelsea, made six changes against the Croatian champions, leaving top scorer Brian Brobbey on the bench along with influential midfielder Enzo Le Fee.

Le Bris also labelled the club's domestic struggles this term as 'growing pains', and Sunderland are not the first promoted club to suffer second-season syndrome. The problem for them is that they also have to contend with a lot more games due to their success last season.

The Black Cats found Dinamo, who parted company with domestic double-winning manager Mario Kovacevic following a shock defeat by newly-promoted Rudes on Saturday, hard to break down in the first 15 minutes, and when Chris Rigg did get in behind after being found by captain Granit Xhaka, Jules Ahoka could not get enough power on his header.

Dinamo's Stojkovic, however, could not have hit his effort at the other end of the pitch any better. With Wilson Isidor waiting to come back on the pitch following treatment, the visitors, backed by 1,500 noisy fans, won a corner. Xhaka headed it away from goal, but only as far as Stojkovic, who chested the ball down and superbly volleyed it past Robin Roefs to put Dinamo ahead.

Thomas Meunier then clipped the woodwork with a cross aimed for the head of Isidor before things got even worse for the home side. Kevin Danso's weak clearance found Stojkovic, who clipped the ball to Beljo, who then dinked it over Roefs to put his team in control at the break.

Le Fee was one of four players sent on by Le Bris for the second half, and a goal from Isidor - he headed Xhaka's free-kick home - was ruled out for offside a minute after the restart.

Sunderland, at least, were playing with some much-needed urgency following a lacklustre first 45 minutes, and Danso hit the crossbar during a spell of pressure from Le Bris's side.

Sunderland fans vented their frustration, both at their team and referee Andrea Colombo, as the second half wore on.

Luka Stojkovic scored Dinamo Zagreb's opener in their 2-0 win with this sublime strike

But Sunderland, for all their second-half possession, rarely tested goalkeeper Dominik Kotarski, Dinamo saw the game out to condemn Sunderland to only their second defeat in European competition, the last having come against Sporting Lisbon in the 1973-74 season.

Le Bris must now quickly pick up his side ahead of the visit of Chelsea.

Progression in Europe is important for the club, and Sunderland should still avoid elimination when the Europa League's group phase ends, but nowhere near as important as preserving its Premier League status.

Forget the icing on the cake, the Cherries joint-top, second on goal difference, of the Europa League after their come-from-behind 3-1 win at Sparta Prague.

After winning just one of their opening eight matches in all competitions, Bournemouth have now won seven on the bounce thanks to second-half goals from Tyler Adams, Evanilson and Rayan. All three came on as second-half substitutes to underline the quality that Marco Rose has at his disposal.

'You can't get too comfortable. You have to continue to hold that standard,' reflected Adams post-match. 'That winning mentality becomes continuous, especially when you're playing every three days.'

Rose, who made eight changes to his XI, will be delighted with his side's fight but will also thank Sparta centre-back Tobias Guddal who inexplicably got himself sent off in the first half for two avoidable yellow cards.

Prior to Guddal's red card, Sparta were in the ascendancy and should have taken the lead when striker Jonatan Braut Brunes, Erling Haaland's cousin, inexplicably put wide a tap-in in the opening two minutes.

That was the biggest chance in the match until Bournemouth were awarded a penalty midway through the first half. Former Liverpool defender Ki-Jana Hoever, who is on loan from Wolves, was booked for a handball in the box. Lewis Cook's stutter run-up fooled Jakub Surovcik but saw his low effort hit the inside of the left-hand post before rolling out of play.

Evanilson was on the scoresheet as Bournemouth came from behind to win at Sparta Prague

Fellow substitute Tyler Adams (second left) started the visitors' 3-1 comeback with this finish

Rayan celebrates after adding a third for Bournemouth to complete their memorable victory

If Cook was unlucky, there was no element of luck to Sparta breaking the deadlock. Counter-attacking from a Cherries' corner, Surovcik threw the ball out to Ebrima Singhateh inside his own half. The impressive winger shrugged off Cook before beginning his brilliant run, which included slaloming in between Bournemouth players, and scoring. It was a goal befitting of the Champions League, let alone the Europa League.

Sparta's joy was short-lived as Guddal, who had already been booked for a foul on Ben Gannon-Doak, then inexplicably brought down Alvaro Rodriguez.

Rose turned to his bench at half-time and all of his changes worked as they pressed Sparta into mistakes. Adams was the beneficiary for their first goal as he scored with a low right-footed shot from outside the box 12 minutes after coming on.

With 10 minutes remaining Evanilson put the visitors ahead with a sublime curled effort into the far corner with no backlift.

'He's on fire right now, but you see him do it every day in training,' Adams purred about his team-mate. For him to do it in a game is no surprise. He has so much quality.

'Whenever he gets in and around the box, we're confident he's going to find the back of the net.'

Ebrima Singhateh scored the goal of the game to give Sparta the lead after a stunning solo run

Before Singhateh's stunner, Lewis Cook saw his penalty hit the inside of the post and go out

Evanilson then turned provider, via a neat one-two, to see Rayan score from distance.

The result means it's four out of four in the Europa League for the European debutants. With Celta Vigo away next after the international break, don't be surprised if it's five out of five.

As the fourth official signalled three minutes of added time, Pierre Sage may have been cursing his luck on the Selhurst Park touchline.

Although he has been hampered by the absences of Jean-Philippe Mateta, Ismaila Sarr and Dean Henderson at points this season, plus a transfer strategy that has left him shorn of experience and quality in key areas, the Frenchman was approaching a record of eight defeats in 13 league and European games.

Two seasons ago, Crystal Palace's hierarchy kept faith with Oliver Glasner when his side won one of their first 13 matches - a record that preceded the greatest 18 months in the club's history - but Sage was running out of time to prove he deserved a similar demonstration of trust.

Enter Daichi Kamada, Palace's best player here, as he finished calmly through the legs of Hoffenheim goalkeeper Oliver Baumann to rescue a valuable point for his side.

But this was a let-off for Sage on a night that had felt like it could precede the final days of his tenure, and he must now summon an improved display against Liverpool this weekend.

'Conceding early in the game was difficult because we had to push to come back,' Sage said post-match. 'But we scored at the end, and the players deserved it because they didn't give up.'

Daichi Kamara earned Crystal Palace a point in second-half stoppage-time against Hoffenheim

Hoffenheim took the lead in the 1-1 encounter when Alexander Prass (second right) scored

Palace's equaliser came when down to 10 men after Adam Wharton's (centre) earlier dismissal

There was nothing to sum up Palace's predicament quite like Alexander Prass' early opener. Having started well - with Kamada having a goal ruled out for offside - Quinten Timber saw a penalty appeal waved away before the out-of-form Adam Wharton was dispossessed. The German side broke forward at electric speed and Prass' effort squirmed through Henderson.

It was an all too familiar story as Palace's defence - weakened by Sage's decision to leave Axel Disasi out of his squad in what he later labelled 'an internal decision' - again looked ill-equipped for the challenge in hand.

'Offensively we did better than our two previous games, but we have to continue to improve defensively because we gave too much space to them,' Sage added.

'When we defend too much, we have no chance to exist in the game, and when we try to attack a little bit, we are quickly open. You don't exist in the game when you don't attack. For this team the best way to defend is to keep the ball with efficiency.'

The hosts were careless on the ball though, doing little to improve the subdued atmosphere at Selhurst Park, and although Yeremy Pino and Kamada spurned good chances, Hoffenheim appeared to have closed out the game.

Palace's late equaliser eases the pressure on under-fire boss Pierre Sage for now

Palace's frustration was demonstrated by four yellow cards in seven minutes, before Wharton received a second shortly after to compound their misery.

The home faithful threatened to turn restless and it looked like the night would end in disappointment, until Kamada's strike gave Sage a lifeline.

Trust Pascal Gross to seize the moment. For a little over an hour, Brighton toiled and laboured in pursuit of the goal that would ignite their European dreams.

The Seagulls have made light work of the Premier League, these vanquishers of Arsenal and Manchester City and now are starting to stretch their dominance across the continent.

Gnarly minnows Getafe love to make life deeply unpleasant for their opponents and Brighton, for all their energy and endeavour, looked destined to be unable to find the answers.

Yet there he was, this 35-year-old starting a remarkable 16th straight game of the season when it mattered. There was Gross, afforded too much space on the left, allowed to spot the run of Joao Costinha towards the back post.

Naturally, the German landed his raking cross right on Costinha's head. The wing-back nodded it across goal for Malick Yalcouye to send a header of his own into the top corner to win it and send Brighton, who are yet to concede in the competition, into the Conference League play-off places and their fans dreaming of European glory.

'The fans should dream and, hopefully at one point, maybe we fulfil their dream,' said Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler.

Malick Yalcouye (centre) scored the winner as Brighton won 1-0 at Getafe in the Europa Conference League

'We focus on work and we focus on the things we can control. We didn't play our best game. We had a few moments where we were lazy with the easy things. We didn't do the simple things on the highest level. But we kept a clean sheet, scored in the right moment and I think we deserve to win this game.'

Getafe, this modest club from the outskirts of Madrid, have long lived in the shadow of their monumental neighbours Real and Atletico but have also earned a famous reputation for a good old-fashioned giant killing.

They once beat Barcelona 4-0 here to overturn a three-goal deficit to reach the Copa del Rey final and then did them again in the league the following season. They went up the road to the Bernabeu in March and came away with three points.

Brighton, meanwhile, have made such a habit of turning over the bigger boys that, for the Seagulls, it's stopped becoming that extraordinary.

They mix so frequently among the giants these days that it's often easy to see the Seagulls as ones themselves. Getafe certainly would.

What was always going to be fascinating was the clash of styles. Brighton, with their relentless press and free-flowing football under Fabian Hurzeler, against a physical Getafe side that boasts the lowest possession and pass success rate in La Liga. There's a reason their players have already been shown six red cards

They certainly made it awkward for Brighton at times here. Bart Verbruggen was twice called upon to deny Getafe striker Ivan Azon in the first half – initially after some chaos inside the Brighton box and secondly after a desperately poor back pass from Olivier Boscagli on the stroke of the break.

Unlike in their Premier League exploits, Hurzeler's side struggled to find that bit of quality when it mattered.

Georginio Rutter, in his first start since August, fizzed a cross to the back post but it eluded Yasin Ayari, the hero of the Eithad, and then fired a shot of his own wide.

Heaven only knows how the ball didn't end up in the net when Jaouen Hadjam, Brighton's brightest spark, raced through on goal but couldn't beat the keeper or the post and Yalcouye's rebound couldn't find the gaping goalmouth.

Hadjam flicked the top of the crossbar with another effort in the second half before substitute Luka Vuskovic blazed another over.

Thankfully, as so often is the case, Gross was there to make it count.

#1634. Man City transfer news: Etihad player ‘finished’ under Enzo Maresca with January plans revealed

By Oliver Thomas | 09 Nov 2026 13:56

Manchester City defender Rayan Ait-Nouri is reportedly ‘finished’ at the Etihad Stadium having fallen down the pecking order under manager Enzo Maresca.

Ait-Nouri was signed by Maresca’s predecessor Pep Guardiola in the summer of 2025, joining from Wolverhampton Wanderers in a £31m deal and penning a five-year contract.

The 25-year-old left-back chipped in with five assists in 28 appearances for City across all competitions last season, missing the majority of December and January following his involvement with Algeria at the Africa Cup of Nations.

Ait-Nouri celebrated winning both the FA Cup and EFL Cup in his debut campaign with the Sky Blues, though he did not feature in either final played at Wembley.

This term, Ait-Nouri has struggled to force his way into Maresca’s first-team plans and is currently viewed as a third-choice left-back behind Josko Gvardiol and Nico O'Reilly.

Ait-Nouri is yet to make a single Premier League appearance for Man City in 2026-27, while he has made just two substitute appearances in the Champions League – his only two starts have come in the EFL Cup.

Although Ait-Nouri is said to remain keen to fight for his place at Man City, Football Insider claims that the defender has failed to make an impression under Maresca.

The report adds that Ait-Nouri is unlikely to play ahead of either Gvardiol or O’Reilly any time soon, and could therefore push for a move away from City during the January transfer window in search of regular first-team football.

Maresca recently admitted that Ait-Nouri is struggling for game time, telling reporters: "He's a clear full-back. In that position, we have [Gvardiol], who is doing fantastic, we have [O'Reilly], who when he is fit is doing fantastic; and he's the same position, so it's just competition between them."

A surprise transfer to City’s rivals Manchester United was mooted for Ait-Nouri in the closing stages of the summer window, and the possibility of the Red Devils making a January swoop is said to have been explored.

While agreeing personal terms would seemingly not be an issue for Ait-Nouri, who could be receptive to a switch across Manchester, it is understood that the relationship between City and United is the ‘main issue’ that could scupper this potential move.

Serie A giants Juventus have also been consistently linked with a move for Ait-Nouri and a switch to Italy is thought to be more realistic at this stage, though the Old Lady may prefer to negotiate an initial loan deal.

#1633. Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3. The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

VEGF is frequently targeted in clinical settings to suppress tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and retina disease6. However, resistance to VEGF-blocking antibodies arises over time, which limits the effectiveness of such treatments4,5,7,8. By contrast, resistance to loss of VEGF signalling has not been reported during physiological vascular development.

Embryos or postnatal tissues lacking activity of the VEGF signalling pathway in all cells fail to develop vessels3. VEGFR2 (encoded by the Kdr (also known as Vegfr2) gene in mice) is the most important VEGF receptor and has been shown to be essential for angiogenesis in all vascular development contexts studied so far1,9. Germline mutants for this gene completely lack blood vessels and die very early during embryonic development2, and mouse embryos chimeras formed by wild-type and Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) progenitor cells cannot form endothelial cells (ECs)10. Conditional deletion of Vegfr2 with Tie2–Cre after endothelial differentiation11, or in postnatal tissues with Cdh5–CreERT2, also strongly impairs angiogenesis12, without any evidence of genetic compensation or resistance.

Despite a large body of literature showing that VEGFR2 is essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, migration and survival, previous studies involving deletion of Vegfr2 in all ECs (Vegfr2iDEC) during embryonic or postnatal organ development could only analyse its effect on angiogenesis for a relatively short period of time. Its essential role in vascular development and hence in tissue development and organ function causes severe impairment of angiogenesis and premature lethality of Vegfr2iDEC embryos and postnatal animals; thus, such studies have been unable to determine whether ECs can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 over time or make certain organ vascular beds in the complete absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling.

Here we used iFlpMosaics13 and iSuRe–HadCre14 to mosaically induce and longitudinally track Vegfr2KO ECs, enabling us to assess the role of this gene during the entire embryonic and postnatal vascular development of different organs. We found that despite its essential role during the initial wave of embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is dispensable for many subsequent angiogenic processes originating from veins. Vegfr2KO ECs expand and out-compete wild-type ECs in venous vessels, which serve as a continuous source of these mutant cells for angiogenesis in most organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) showed that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time through upregulation of ligands for other VEGF receptors and through increased expression of venous-specific genes, particularly Nr2f2. Targeting these adaptive and resistance-associated molecular mechanisms prevents expansion of ECs following prolonged loss of VEGFR2 signalling.

Given the essential role of VEGFR2 in early angiogenesis and embryonic development, we induced mosaic loss of VEGFR2 with iFlpMosaics13 to investigate whether mutant cells could adapt and form new vessels over time. This technology enables FlpO-dependent ratiometric induction and tracking over long periods of time of cells expressing MTomato-2A-Cre (knockout for any floxed gene) or MYFP (wild type). To induce these mosaics, we used the Apln-FlpO allele, which is expressed in the first angiogenic and sprouting ECs at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) and throughout vascular development. In female embryos, the X-chromosome-located Apln–FlpO allele is mosaically silenced15 and expressed only in a fraction (23–50%) of ECs, generating relatively few mutant and wild-type cells, which we found to be compatible with embryonic development (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a). Analysis of major organs of Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic mice showed that ECs with full loss of VEGFR2 (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) were able to survive and proliferate during embryonic development and until postnatal day 7 (P7), with only a relatively minor competitive disadvantage (2–7-fold) compared with wild-type cells (Fig. 1b). This competitive disadvantage was more pronounced in the lung and kidney endothelium and less so in brain ECs (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). As Apln-FlpO is constitutively active and can drive recombination at later stages of embryonic development, we also induced Vegfr2 deletion using 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at E10.5 and E12.5 in embryos carrying Cdh5-CreERT2, iSuRe-HadCre and an iMb2-Mosaic16 control reporter that recombines independently of Vegfr2 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). This resulted in a maximum of 1–6% recombined ECs, as opposed to 23–50% with Apln-FlpO. However, this recapitulated the trend in which brain ECs were least affected by VEGFR2 loss, followed by those in the heart, liver, lung and kidney (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

a, Schematic of iFlpMosaics induced by Apln-FlpO from E8.5 to P7. b, log2 ratio of MTomato+/MYFP+ within CD31+CD45− cells detected by FACS for the indicated organs. The absolute fold change of the ratio of Vegfr2KO ECs versus the ratio of control Tomato+ cells is indicated in red. c, Representative gating scheme for the ratiometric analysis (see also Extended Data Fig. 1a). d, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 retinas immunostained for Tomato, YFP and ERG (which labels EC nuclei). Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing the zonal distribution and percentage of Tomato+Cre+ cells when equal numbers of randomly selected YFP+ and Tomato+ cells were plotted (see method in Extended Data Fig. 3a). Right, log2 ratio of Tomato+/YFP+ cells detected in whole-mount retina immunostainings, showing an overall competitive disadvantage of Vegfr2KO cells in the mapped retinas. e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for ERG at P7, from pups injected with 4-OHT at P1. Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing distribution of MTomato+ERG+ (wild-type, Vegfr2HET or Vegfr2KO) cells in space in relation to MTomato−ERG+ (wild-type) cells. f, Bar plot contrasting the relative frequency of the indicated cells in the indicated areas and genotypes. g, log2 fold change of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 cells relative to the respective control wild-type cells. Numbers indicate fold change (×) between the two groups. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm. A, arteries; AF, angiogenic front; dist., distance; freq., frequency; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; LE, leading edge; MA, mature area; V, veins; WT, wild type.

VEGFR2 activity is essential for NOTCH activation and the development of arteries17,18,19. Arteries are formed by tip ECs20, which have the highest level of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling and guide vascular growth. Our high-resolution spatial zonation data with long-term iFlpMosaics showed that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were significantly enriched in veins and surrounding capillaries, and avoided angiogenic front capillaries or tip ECs, but were able to form arteries (Fig. 1d; see also Extended Data Fig. 3a for the heatmapping method).

To complement these results, we intercrossed the Vegfr2 floxed allele with Cdh5-CreERT2 and iSuRe-HadCre14 alleles to ensure fast (24 h; Extended Data Fig. 3b,c) and effective mosaic genetic deletion and full loss of VEGFR2 protein and downstream targets in ECs (Cdh5 expressing), after a single injection of 4-OHT. Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs were located mainly in veins and surrounding capillaries, as well as in the more proximal and mature segments of retina arteries (Fig. 1e). This indicates that when Vegfr2KO ECs are induced in the initial retina sprouting plexus at P1, they can make arteries forming from P1 to P3. However, owing to their inability to continue to sprout and form tip cells at the leading edge, they cannot participate in the subsequent arterial development process occurring from P3 to P7, which in the retina is dependent on incorporation of new tip cells21.

Notably, compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1−P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front capillaries (Fig. 1f,g) and were still able to make arteries. This suggests that embryonic Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs can adapt to long-term loss of VEGFR2 and contribute to venous vascular growth, tip cells and arteries at postnatal stages.

We next investigated how Vegfr2KO ECs could compete with wild-type cells and contribute to growing vascular networks over long periods of time, given the proposed important role of this pathway in EC proliferation1,22. During angiogenesis, there are two main locations for EC proliferation: the capillary angiogenic front and veins (Fig. 2a). We found that the surviving Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs proliferated (as determined by Ki-67 detection) as well as wild-type cells in postnatal brain, heart and lung vessels (Fig. 2b).

a, Representative confocal micrograph of a control P7 retina immunostained for the proliferation marker Ki-67 and the EC nuclear marker ERG. The chart shows the frequency of Ki-67+ERG+ (pink pseudocolored) nuclei in different vascular zones. b, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 mice at P7, immunostained for YFP, Tomato, ERG and Ki-67. Yellow arrows indicate YFP+Ki-67+ cells and magenta arrows Tomato+Ki-67+ ECs. c, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 retinas induced at P1 and analysed at P20. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing that Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 ECs grow in veins and surrounding capillaries. d,e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for cleaved caspase 3 and respective quantification charts, showing increased apoptosis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 but not Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs. f, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice induced at P4 and analysed at P7. Arrows indicate recombined ECs (Tomato+) that are Ki-67+ (yellow) and Ki-67− (white), respectively. Chart shows the percentage of Tomato+ ECs positive for Ki-67. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm (a,c–e), 50 μm (b,f). Cap., capillaries; CC3, cleaved caspase 3; Ctrl, control; DCap, distal capillaries; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; PCap, proximal capillaries. *Adjusted P < 0.05.

Venous ECs provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis and these migrate against the blood flow to capillaries and then towards arterial vessels20,23,24. When we induced Vegfr2KO ECs for longer periods of time, from P1 to P20 (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20), we observed that mutant cells stayed in the vein stem, where they proliferated and gradually outcompeted wild-type cells, which moved outwards towards the VEGF-rich leading edge and adjacent capillaries (Fig. 2c). This preferential occupation of the venous stem niche by Vegfr2KO ECs allowed them to continue proliferating for longer periods of time and later to form most of the perivenous capillary vessels and the deeper vascular plexus that developed during a second wave of VEGF-independent angiogenesis from P7 to P20 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). This was consistent with previous findings showing that the tip cells that dive to form the deeper vascular plexus in the retina lack expression of the VEGFR2 signalling target gene Esm1; instead, their migration is dependent on other pathways such as Alk or TGFβ and WNT signalling25,26,27.

Together, these data show that VEGFR2 function is essential for the initial sprouting angiogenesis driven by high VEGF levels in hypoxic embryos and organs but not for the development of veins and perivenous capillaries or the subsequent steps of capillary angiogenesis and remodelling that occur after the first vascular plexus is formed in various organs. Thus, by forming veins, which are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis23, Vegfr2KO ECs can continue to proliferate and participate in subsequent steps of vascular development for long periods of time.

We previously observed that the distribution of Vegfr2KO ECs in the retina plexus at P7 differed between animals with long-term (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) and short-term (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7) mosaic deletion of Vegfr2. Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front than Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs (Fig. 1f,g). Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs also proliferated normally (Fig. 2b). Therefore, we hypothesized that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs might be genetically rewired and adapt over time to loss of the most important receptor for VEGF.

To assess the early response of ECs to loss of VEGFR2, we first analysed apoptosis markers in growing retina vessels, as VEGFR2 has been shown to regulate EC survival. Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice showed a very significant increase in the number of apoptotic (cleaved caspase 3 positive) ECs (Fig. 2d). This apoptosis was a reaction to the acute loss of VEGFR2, as Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 or even Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 mice did not show any apoptotic ECs (Fig. 2e), suggesting adaptation of the surviving cells over time. When the acute loss of Vegfr2 was induced in all ECs, we observed an immediate depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs from the VEGF-high angiogenic front, but not from veins or more mature vessels (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Therefore, even though many ECs in the retina plexus showed upregulation of the apoptosis marker in the first days after Vegfr2 loss (Fig. 2d), only the angiogenic ECs that were exposed to high VEGF levels at the time of Vegfr2 deletion died (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

We also found that Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs were significantly less proliferative than control cells only in the heart and kidney (Fig. 2f), whereas the proliferation of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was similar to that of controls (Fig. 2b). This suggests that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time and are later able to proliferate in these organs. In the newborn retina, deletion of Vegfr2 did not affect the proliferation of surviving ECs in any segment (Extended Data Fig. 4d), indicating that in this organ VEGFR2 mainly controls EC migration and survival, not proliferation.

Together, our data suggest that ECs lacking VEGF signalling during active angiogenesis suffer an acute VEGFR2 withdrawal effect, followed by a period of adaptation to the loss, after which they can form new vessels. ECs that are more distant from the VEGF source, and therefore have less VEGF signalling, adapt better to the loss and can expand over time, particularly in veins and perivenous vessels.

To further confirm the insensitivity of more mature ECs to loss of VEGFR2 signalling, we deleted Vegfr2 in several adult quiescent vascular beds for 2 weeks. Only the quiescent sinusoidal liver endothelium showed a strong sensitivity and loss of Vegfr2KO ECs, whereas only the kidney endothelium showed significantly lower proliferation (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting that only fenestrated or discontinuous mature endothelial vessels present in these organs remain sensitive to VEGFR2 loss.

Given the observed differences in the biology of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of these cells and respective control Tomato+ cells to identify possible differences in their transcriptional profiles and potential mechanisms of adaptation to loss of VEGFR2 signalling in distinct organ vascular beds.

Although VEGFR2 is a central regulator of angiogenesis and widely regarded as essential for EC biology, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs showed only modest changes in their transcriptome (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6), even though VEGFR2 protein and downstream signalling were lost already within the first 24 h following 4-OHT administration (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). In general, the expression of genes related to sprouting or tip cell biology was decreased, whereas that of genes related to apoptosis and vascular permeability was increased in all organs analysed (Fig. 3a,b). However, considerable differences were observed among organs.

For volcano plots and heatmaps (a,b,g,i,n,p), statistical analyses used Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. For hallmark pathways (h,o), statistical analyses used the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea) and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple testing. *Adjusted P < 0.05.

In the brain, clusters of proliferating (S–G2–M) ECs expressing venous capillaries markers were increased after Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days (Fig. 3c–f). This was consistent with higher clonal expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs from P1 to P20 in this organ (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Clusters comprising capillary and activated or angiogenic ECs (with high expression of Apln, Adm, Mcam, Lamb1 and Angpt2) were decreased (Fig. 3d–f). In total, only 569 genes were significantly deregulated (Fig. 3g). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed an increase in the expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as G2M, DNA repair and mitotic spindle genes, confirming the increase in EC proliferation (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a). The expression of most tip cell marker genes was decreased in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 6a–f).

In contrast to those in the brain, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 capillary ECs in the heart were significantly less proliferative (Fig. 3j–m and Extended Data Fig. 7b), matching the 54% decrease in Ki-67 percentage observed in sections (Fig. 2f). The proportion of mutant ECs found in bigger vessels (arteries and veins) was increased 2- to 4-fold (Fig. 3k–m), suggesting a proportional fast depletion of Vegfr2KO capillary ECs in only 3 days. Unlike in the brain, GSEA of Vegfr2KO heart ECs showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as decreases in expression of G2M, mitotic spindle and tip cell genes (Fig. 3n–p), in accordance with the decrease in proliferation and sprouting of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 heart ECs. Vegfr2KO heart ECs also showed upregulation of genes related to apoptosis and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Fig. 3n–p), as has been shown previously for ECs losing ERK signalling28.

In contrast to the results for brain and heart, we found no significant difference in the proportions of proliferating cells among control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs in lung (Extended Data Fig. 6g–j), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 and clonal analysis (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7c). The proportion of the vein cluster was only slightly increased, and the capillary cluster was slightly decreased. Despite the lack of significant changes in cluster proportions, GSEA showed increased TNF signalling through NF-κB, hypoxia and reactive oxygen species signalling and a decrease in the interferon response (Extended Data Fig. 6k,l). In lung, there was only a small trend of decreased expression of tip cell marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 6m), and several genes related to apoptosis were upregulated (Extended Data Fig. 6l,m).

In the kidney, similar to the heart, Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days led to an increase in the relative proportion of ECs of bigger vessels (arteries and veins), suggesting fast depletion of a fraction of capillary ECs in only 3 days (Extended Data Fig. 6n–q). Proliferation and clonal expansion of kidney capillary ECs were also reduced (Extended Data Figs. 6o,q and 7d), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 (Fig. 2f). GSEA showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F, G2M and mitotic spindle genes and an increase in the expression of genes related to p53, xenobiotic metabolism and apoptosis (Extended Data Fig. 6r,s), indicative of cellular stress in kidney ECs after short-term Vegfr2 deletion from P4 to P7. Similar to brain and heart ECs, the expression of tip cell marker genes was also decreased in kidney Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 6t).

Following our analysis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs of distinct organs to identify potential differences in gene expression related to long-term adaptation of cells to loss of VEGFR2 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). In contrast to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs exhibited predominantly upregulation rather than downregulation of genes, including marked upregulation of several venous-enriched genes (compare Figs. 3a,b and 4a).

In contrast to brain Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had increased frequencies of venous capillaries (Extended Data Fig. 8b–d) and marked upregulation of the key regulator of vein specification Nr2f2 (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Similarly to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had decreased frequencies of activated and sprouting ECs and lower expression levels of several tip cell genes (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). The number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), particularly upregulated genes, was much higher (1,621 versus 569 DEGs) in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs; this is likely to represent a long-term adaptation response to loss of VEGFR2 function (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e with Fig. 3g). Whereas in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs, genetic pathways related to EC proliferation and cellular activity (E2F targets, MYC, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis) were paradoxically increased, in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs they were decreased (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e,f with Fig. 3g,h). This suggests that brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs adapt to the long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling through a decrease in cellular activity and upregulation of Nr2f2, which probably decreases their dependence on VEGF signalling for growth and survival.

In the heart, we confirmed previous histological analysis showing that heart Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs proliferated at levels similar to those of control cells and markedly higher than those of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (compare Fig. 3k,m with Fig. 4b–d). They also had many more DEGs (1,750 DEGs versus 242 DEGs), particularly upregulated genes (compare Fig. 3n with Fig. 4e). GSEA showed increased epithelial–mesenchymal transition, KRAS signalling and angiogenesis, and less expression of metabolic-pathway-related genes (Fig. 4e,f), as seen in the brain. Expression of tip or activated EC genes was not as compromised in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Fig. 4g), suggesting some adaptation over time to the loss of VEGFR2. Notably, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4c,d), similar to our observations in the retina (Fig. 1d–f), confirming that mosaic loss of Vegfr2 causes mutant ECs to expand more in veins. In comparison with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed strong upregulation of most venous-specific genes, including Nr2f2, Fbln2, Igf1 and Vwf (Fig. 4e). This was not caused only by the increased proportion of venous ECs in these mutants; capillary and angiogenic ECs also showed much higher expression of these venous marker genes, indicating venousization of mutant Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 capillary ECs over time (Fig. 4h,p).

In the lung, the same adaptation and venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was observed. Mutant cells were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4i–k), and even capillary or CAR4+ ECs showed significantly upregulated expression of lung venous genes including Vegfc, Nr2f2, Vwf and Fbln2 (Fig. 4l,m and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Similar to findings in the other organs, lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had significantly more DEGs than lung Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (3,116 vs 502), particularly upregulated genes (compare Extended Data Fig. 6k with Fig. 4m). Volcano plots and GSEA revealed upregulation of many venous-enriched and epithelial–mesenchymal transition genes, as well as oestrogen response genes. Lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had lower expression of E2F targets and metabolism genes, as seen in the other organs (Fig. 4m,n).

Notably, deletion of Vegfr2 for 2 weeks in adult organ blood vessels did not induce venousization of adult Vegfr2KO ECs; instead, it decreased expression of venous genes (Extended Data Fig. 8g–u), indicating that upregulation of Nr2f2 and venousization may represent a long-term adaptative response to VEGFR2 loss that occurs only during active angiogenesis.

The scRNA-seq data indicating venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs over time were confirmed by immunostaining for the master regulator of venous development NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII) (Fig. 4o,p and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). To understand the venousization requirement for long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs, we also analysed Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic Vegfr2Flox/Flox, Nr2f2Flox/Flox mice. When ECs lacked both VEGFR2 and NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), their capacity to expand was significantly reduced, particularly in veins (Fig. 4q,r and Extended Data Fig. 9e). This suggests that endothelial venousization is a key mechanism of adaptation to long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis that enables mutant cells to expand in veins and derived vessels over time.

In addition to analysing embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, we tested the capacity of Vegfr2KO ECs to form tumour vessels over a period of 2 weeks. When Vegfr2 deletion was induced a few days before tumour implantation, Vegfr2IECKO-day-3–adult ECs formed tumour vessels mainly at the tumour border and failed to penetrate deeper into the tumour, where they were 5.2-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10a). By contrast, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–adult ECs, which had undergone venousization throughout embryonic and postnatal development, could better reach inside the tumour and were only 2.6-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). These data show that although VEGFR2 signalling promotes tumour angiogenesis, ECs can progressively adapt to its absence and sustain tumour angiogenesis.

In addition to our findings with respect to venousization, we observed significant upregulation of expression of other VEGF receptor ligands in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11a), including PGF and VEGFC, which bind and activate VEGFR1 and VEGFR3, respectively1. In the absence of VEGFR2, VEGFR1 is the only other receptor that can bind VEGFA. However, all studies so far have shown that VEGFR1 kinase activity is too weak29,30, whereas its extracellular soluble form (sVEGFR1 or sFLT1) acts as a strong VEGF decoy receptor31. Therefore, when VEGFR2 is present, VEGFR1 is considered to mainly antagonize VEGFA–VEGFR2 signalling and angiogenesis. However, we found that Vegfr1 expression was much higher in ECs in the brain, the organ least sensitive to VEGFR2 loss (Extended Data Fig. 11b). We also found that during postnatal angiogenesis, sVegfr1 showed 2–5-fold lower expression than the membrane full-length Vegfr1 (flVegfr1) mRNA form, except in brain ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11c), suggesting a potential signalling role for flVEGFR1.

To evaluate whether VEGFR1 could compensate for loss of VEGFR2, we induced mosaic codeletion of Vegfr1 and Vegfr2 in ECs with iSuRe-HadCre from P1 to P7 (Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1–P7). Compared with Vegfr2KO ECs, Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed a further decrease in ability to migrate and form retina capillaries, but not veins or arteries (Fig. 5a). In veins, Vegfr1/2KO ECs could clonally expand (Extended Data Fig. 11d). Brain and heart Vegfr1/2KO ECs proliferated less than Vegfr2KO ECs at P7 (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Deletion of both Vegfr2 and Vegfr1 had a stronger effect on endothelial and pup survival (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i), confirming the requirement for VEGFR1 signalling when VEGFR2 is absent in capillaries. Mosaic deletion of Vegfr1 alone also led to a decrease in EC migration towards the VEGF-rich front (Extended Data Fig. 11j). In contrast to deletion of Vegfr1 in all ECs, mosaic loss of Vegfr1 in single ECs did not increase VEGF signalling (as assessed by ESM1 expression), probably owing to normal levels of sFLT1 present in the mostly wild-type microenvironment (Extended Data Fig. 11k).

In addition to VEGFR1 and VEGFR2, ECs express VEGFR3. Previous studies have shown that VEGFR3 is strongly expressed by capillary and venous ECs; however, this receptor cannot bind VEGF (VEGFA), only VEGFC and VEGFD, which are key molecules for lymphangiogenesis but less relevant to blood vessel angiogenesis. Vegfr2IECKO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed very strong upregulation of VEGFC (Extended Data Fig. 11a), which could signal to VEGFR3 in the absence of VEGFR2. Loss of VEGFR3 in growing retina ECs has been shown to induce angiogenesis, suggesting that VEGFR3 negatively regulates VEGFR2 signalling32. However, single Vegfr3IECKO-P1–P7 ECs also had decreased ability to migrate and reach the leading edge (Extended Data Fig. 11l–n). Arterial ECs and smooth muscle cells express high levels of VEGFC33,34,35 a ligand that can bind both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3. Compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, Vegfr2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs had a very similar zonal distribution in capillaries and veins (Fig. 5b) but a 3.4-fold lower frequency in arteries (Fig. 5c); this suggests an important role for VEGFC to VEGFR3 signalling in arterial mobilization or survival, but only when VEGFR2 signalling is absent. Loss of both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 did not compromise the proliferation of surviving ECs in any vascular segments (Fig. 5d).

We also observed that Vegfr2KO ECs had decreased VEGFR3 expression only at the angiogenic front, where VEGFA levels are highest. By contrast Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed strong downregulation of VEGFR3 in all vascular segments, except in arteries (Fig. 5e). Vegfr1/2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs behaved similarly to Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, except for a pronounced decrease in formation of arterial vessels (Fig. 5f–h). Taken together, our findings show that in the absence of VEGFR2 signalling, VEGFR1 is required to sustain VEGFR3 expression and growth and migration of capillary ECs. In arteries, VEGFR3 continues to be expressed after loss of VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 and regulates development of arteries when the other VEGFA receptors are missing. Notably, vein ECs can survive and clonally expand in the complete absence of all VEGF receptor signalling (Fig. 5i).

Our study challenges the longstanding view that VEGFR2 signalling is indispensable for endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting during angiogenesis1,22. By using iFlpMosaics to induce ratiometric genetic mosaics of wild-type and Vegfr2KO ECs, we demonstrated that these mutant cells are capable of surviving, proliferating and competing with wild-type ECs during the entire embryonic and postnatal organ growth period (Extended Data Fig. 12). Contrary to previous studies suggesting that VEGFR2 is required for all forms of vascular differentiation and development10,12,36, our findings indicate that VEGFR2-independent mechanisms support angiogenesis in certain vascular beds, particularly the long-term development of venous and perivenous capillaries.

We identified significant organ-specific differences in adaptation to acute loss of VEGFR2 signalling (Extended Data Fig. 12a), thereby extending previous findings37,38. Whereas angiogenic retina ECs were strongly affected, brain ECs were the least affected, retaining high angiogenic potential, partially because of VEGFR1 compensation (Extended Data Fig. 12b). By contrast, postnatal heart, kidney and liver ECs were more sensitive to acute withdrawal of VEGFR2, showing partial depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs in capillaries, as well as a partial reduction in proliferation. The postnatal lung showed a distinct response, with no major changes in EC proliferation or cluster composition but instead a shift in transcriptional programs towards inflammation and metabolic adaptations. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of endothelial responses across different vascular beds and suggest that organ-specific factors influence EC resilience to perturbations in VEGF signalling.

The long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs was a notable observation. Although these cells initially had a competitive disadvantage during early embryonic and postnatal sprouting angiogenesis stages, they ultimately expanded and outcompeted wild-type cells in venous and perivenous regions, indicating that alternative pathways support their survival and proliferation in this niche. Veins are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for capillary angiogenesis and later arterialization20,23, and this venous dominance of Vegfr2KO ECs allows them to compete with wild-type cells over time. Our scRNA-seq analysis of different vascular beds further showed that ECs with prolonged loss of VEGFR2 exhibited a significant shift towards a venous transcriptional signature (venousization), marked by upregulation of many venous genes, including Nr2f2, a master regulator of veins development24,39. Vegfr2KONr2f2KO ECs were significantly less able to expand, particularly in veins, showing that venousization is a key adaptation mechanism that enables Vegfr2KO ECs to persist and contribute to vascular development (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d).

In addition to venousization, our findings demonstrate the compensatory roles of VEGFR1 and VEGFR3 in supporting survival and growth signalling when VEGFR2 is absent (Extended Data Fig. 12b). Previously, VEGFR1 has mainly been reported to negatively regulate VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis, because its soluble secreted version sFLT1 or VEGFR1 is a decoy receptor of VEGF1,22. In our mosaic Vegfr1KO and Vegfr1/2KO experiments, sFLT1 levels in the microenvironment were normal; this led us to find that membrane or full-length VEGFR1 acted as a positive regulator of angiogenesis and partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss, supporting both EC survival and migration. The mosaic single loss of VEGFR3 also showed that this receptor was a positive regulator of EC migration towards the leading edge. This was consistent with results obtained using VEGFR3-blocking antibodies40; however, our findings were contrary to results from pan-endothelial Vegfr3KO genetics experiments32 in which the receptor was lost from all ECs. In this case, VEGFC and/or VEGFD bioavailability in the whole body increases, thereby increasing VEGFC–VEGFR2 signalling, whereas in low-frequency Vegfr3KO mosaics this does not occur. In addition, Vegfr2/3KO ECs mobilized less to the angiogenic front and had decreased arterialization when compared with Vegfr2KO ECs. The ability of these alternative VEGF receptors to sustain EC survival, migration and proliferation at the single-cell level indicates potential functional plasticity and compensation within the VEGF signalling network, as suggested previously by studies using classical full-tissue conditional genetics12,32,37.

An important implication of our study is that EC sensitivity to VEGFR2 loss varies depending on the vascular context and the time since the loss. We found that acute loss of VEGFR2 during active angiogenesis resulted in significant EC depletion in the first 3 days, particularly depletion of tip cells and other ECs at the angiogenic front, where VEGF signalling is highest. However, Vegfr2KO ECs in VEGF-low areas and those that had undergone long-term adaptation were able to persist and even contribute to a substantial portion of capillary vessels, particularly those around veins. This suggests that ECs experiencing prolonged VEGFR2 deficiency undergo venousization in VEGF-low areas, enabling them to survive and then grow in the absence of canonical VEGF signalling. Our tumour models showed that Vegfr2KO ECs could form tumour vessels, particularly if they had previously undergone venousization during embryonic angiogenesis. The use of ratiometric and trackable iFlpMosaics was key to obtaining these findings.

Our work may also provide biomarkers and insights into resistance mechanisms to anti-VEGF therapies5,41,42,43. Adaptation of ECs to VEGFR2 loss by engaging alternative venous-related angiogenic pathways may also occur in tumours. If this is confirmed, therapeutic strategies that simultaneously block the compensatory and venous-related pathways identified here may be necessary to overcome resistance to anti-VEGF treatments.

In conclusion, our study reshapes our understanding of VEGFR2-dependent angiogenesis by demonstrating that ECs possess intrinsic mechanisms to adapt to long-term absence of VEGFR2 signalling. The discovery of endothelial venousization and compensatory VEGF receptor signalling provides a new framework for investigation of alternative modes of vascular development and resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

All mouse husbandry and experiments were conducted using protocols approved by local animal ethics committees and authorities (Comunidad Autónoma de Madrid and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid CAM-PROEX 164.8/20, PROEX 293.1/22 and PROEX-288.7/24). The mouse colonies were maintained in racked individual ventilation cages according to current national legislation. The mice had dust- and pathogen-free bedding and sufficient nesting and environmental enrichment material for development of species-specific behaviour. All mice had ad libitum access to food and water in environmental conditions of 45–65% relative humidity, temperatures of 21–24 °C and a 12 h/12 h light–dark cycle. For preservation of animal welfare, mouse health was monitored with an animal health surveillance programme that followed the recommendations of the Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations for specific-pathogen-free facilities

We used Mus musculus lines mostly on the C57BL6 genetic background, with some having a fraction of 129SV, or B6CBAF1 or DBA genetic backgrounds. Mice were backcrossed to C57Bl6 for several generations. To generate mice for analysis, we intercrossed mice aged between 7 weeks and 30 weeks. We did not anticipate any influence of mouse sex on our data, and both female and male mice were analysed. The initial sample size was determined taking into account the ‘3 Rs’ for animal experimentation and the expected experimental variability based on protocols (published and our own; refs. 13 and 14). The final sample size was defined a posteriori after statistical analysis of the data. Sample size and related statistical analysis methods are indicated in the figure legends or source data. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining.

The following mouse lines were used and intercrossed: Tg(Cdh5–CreERT2)44, Tg(iSuRe–HadCre)14, Vegfr2flox (ref. 45), Vegfr1flox (ref. 46), Vegfr3flox (ref. 47) (for this work, we also generated a new Vegfr3flox allele in the Vegfr1/2flox background, as indicated below), Nr2f2flox (ref. 48), iMb2–Mosaic16, Apln–FlpO15 and the iFlpMosaic lines13 (R26-iFlpMTomato-2A-Cre/MYFP and Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic).

To generate a new Vegfr3flox allele combined with Vegfr1/2flox we injected Cas9, donor DNAs containing LoxP sites and guide RNAs (TGTTAAAGACACGCATACCT/AGG and AGATGGGGTGAATAGCTCCG/TGG) into mouse eggs of the Vegfr1/2flox iSuRe–HadCre Cdh5–CreERT2 line. Founders containing LoxP sites flanking exon 1 in the same chromosome were screened by PCR, and inducible Vegfr3 deletion was confirmed by PCR and immunostaining for the VEGFR3 protein (Extended Data Fig. 11l,m).

For induction of CreERT2 activity in adult mice, 1 g tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich, P5648_1G) was dissolved in 50 ml corn oil (stock tamoxifen concentration, 20 mg m−1), and aliquots were stored at −20 °C. Animals received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl of this stock solution (total dose: 2 mg tamoxifen per animal at 80 mg kg−1), as indicated in the figures. To activate recombination in pups, we injected 4-OHT at the indicated stages at a dose of 40 mg kg−1. For double (VEGFR1/2, VEGFR2/3) or triple (VEGFR1/2/3) mutants, 4-OHT was administered to pups at 15 mg kg−1. For activation of recombination during embryogenesis, pregnant dams were induced with 0.25 mg 4-OHT supplemented with 0.125 mg progesterone at E10.5 and E12.5. All mouse lines and primer sequences required for genotyping are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Lewis carcinoma cells were obtained from ATCC and cultured in DMEM (Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1× penicillin–streptomycin and 2 mM glutamine at 37 °C, 5% CO2. The cell medium was changed every other day, and cells were passaged every 3–4 days. Cells were routinely screened for mycoplasma contamination. Cells were used for tumour inoculation when they were at 75–80% confluency. Cells were trypsinized and resuspended in Matrigel solution (Biosciences). Age-matched (15–20 weeks) and sex-matched mice were injected subcutaneously with 5 × 105 tumour cells suspended in Matrigel (Corning, 354234). Mice were euthanized after 15 days, and tumours (less than 2 cm3) were extracted, fixed and processed for immunostaining.

For immunostaining of mouse retinas, eyes were dissected from mouse pups and fixed by incubation with agitation for 20 min in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (diluted from a stock of 16% PFA; EMS 15710). After two washes in PBS (5 min each), retinas were microdissected from the eyes; 4 incisions were made to enable later flat mounting, and the retinas were refixed in 4% PFA for 45 min with agitation. After two washes in PBS, retinas were blocked and permeabilized by incubation for 1 h in PBST (0.3% Triton X-100, 3% FBS and 3% donkey serum in PBS). Samples were then incubated with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) diluted in PBST overnight at 4 °C with agitation. The next day, retinas were washed 5 times for 20 min in PBST diluted 1:2. Then, they were incubated in the same solution for 2 h at room temperature with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2). After washing (3 × 15 min) in PBS containing 0.15% Triton X-100, retinas were washed (2 × 15 min) in PBS and flat mounted in Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated with the Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For collection of organs and histological analysis, mice were euthanized in CO2 chambers, and 10 ml of PBS was injected into the left ventricles, followed by perfusion with 3.7–4% formaldehyde (ITW Reagents, 252931) at pH 7. The explanted organs were postfixed for 2 h in 4% PFA (Thermo Scientific, 043368.9M) in PBS at 4 °C with gentle rotation. After three washes in PBS for 10 min each, the organs were stored overnight in 30% sucrose (Sigma) in PBS. The organs were then embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Sakura) and frozen at −80 °C. Cryosections of 30 µm were cut on a cryostat (Leica), washed three times for 10 min each time in PBS, and blocked and permeabilized in PBS containing 10% donkey serum (Millipore), 10% FBS and 1% Triton X-100. The primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) were diluted in the same buffer and incubated with sections overnight at 4 °C. This step was followed by three 10-min washes in PBS and incubation for 2 h with conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) and 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in PBS at room temperature. After three washes in PBS, the sections were mounted with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated first with the other primary rabbit antibodies, followed by Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then rabbit epitopes blocked with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally incubated with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For confocal scanning, immunostained organ sections or whole-mount retinas were imaged at high resolution with a Leica SP8 Navigator confocal microscope fitted with a ×10 or ×40 objective. Individual fields or tiles of large areas were acquired. All images shown are representative of the results obtained for each group and experiment. Animals were dissected and processed under identical conditions. Phenotypes or signal intensities were compared using images obtained with the same laser excitation and confocal scanner detection settings. We used ImageJ/Fiji v.1.54f to threshold, select and quantify the objects in confocal micrographs.

For arteriovenous mapping of ERG-labelled control and mutant ECs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), a semiautomatic Fiji script (available at https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab) was developed. First, six regions of interest were manually defined by the user: artery, vein, mature capillaries between the established arteries and veins, intermediate capillaries, angiogenic front and leading edge. ERG labelling was used to segment endothelial nuclei and classify each nucleus according to reporter or marker positivity (determined by the percentage of pixels within each nucleus above a given intensity threshold level), and the XY coordinates of nuclei were extracted. Then, arterial, venous, distal and proximal arteriovenous boundaries were defined by the user to determine the relative position of each segmented nucleus to each arteriovenous field boundary; this enabled compilation of data extracted from different arteriovenous fields into a single XY dot plot or heatmap.

The data collected in Fiji were post-analysed in R (v.4.5.2) for generation of graphs representing the spatial distribution of the cells of interest. For the XY plots and heatmaps, samples were randomly subsetted to enable us to display equal numbers of control and mutant cells (MYFP+ versus MTomato+ in the Apln–FlpO, iFlpMosaic background, and MTomato− versus MTomato+ in the Cdh5–CreERT2, iSuRe–HadCre background); this was to make clear the zonation differences between control and mutant cells. For visualization with XY dot plots, 2,000 randomly selected cells of each group were plotted; for the heatmap generation, the maximal number of cells (determined by the cell type (control or mutant) with fewer cells) was used. The percentage of each cell type in each arteriovenous region was calculated given its spatial distribution per field (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

We generated Fiji macro Script_Reporter_MarkerDetection_Mapping.ijm for spatial mapping of ERG and/or quantification of EC colocalization with reporters (MYFP or MTomato) and other markers (Ki-67) as in Figs. 1, 2, 5. R scripts were used for data quantification and heatmapping (Script_Spatial Heatmap; Figs. 1, 2, 5 and Extended Data Figs. 3, 4, 11) and are available at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab). Fiji, Adobe Photoshop CC 24.1.0 and Adobe Illustrator CC v.27.1.1 were used for downstream image processing, analysis and illustration.

To quantify the clonal expansion of single ECs expressing the iSuRe–HadCre and the Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic alleles, we segmented and analysed images with MTomato+H2B-Cherry+, MTomato+H2B-EGFP+ or MTomato+HA-H2B-Cerulean+ signals with the Clone_Identification_Quantification script, deposited at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab/).

Postnatal and adult tissues were dissociated before fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Enzymatic digestion was carried out at 37 °C for 20 min using a solution containing 2.5 mg ml−1 collagenase type I (Thermo Fisher), 2.5 mg ml−1 dispase II (Thermo Fisher) and 50 μg ml−1 DNase I (Roche). Following dissociation, samples were pelleted by centrifugation (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Pellets were gently resuspended in 1× blood lysis buffer (BioLegend, 420301) and incubated on ice for 5 min for lysis of erythroid cells. After lysis, cells were passed through a 70-μm cell strainer and centrifuged again (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Cells were resuspended in antibody incubation solution (PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+, supplemented with 2% dialysed FBS; Biowest, X0515), with primary antibodies (APC rat anti-mouse CD31 and APC-Cy7 anti-CD45; Supplementary Table 2) only or with the addition of Hashtag oligo (HTO) antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) when scRNA-seq was performed. Samples were then incubated at 4 °C with gentle agitation for 20 min.

After immunolabelling, cells were centrifuged (450g, 4 °C, 5 min), washed with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged again and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added immediately before FACS analysis. Cells were analysed using an LSRFortessa cell analyser or sorted using a FACS Aria Cell Sorter (BD Biosciences). For an example of the FACS gating strategy, see Extended Data Fig. 1a. BD FACSDiva v.8.0.1 and FlowJo v.10 were used for data acquisition and analysis.

For RNA-seq analysis, APC rat anti-mouse CD31 (which labels ECs), APC-Cy7 rat anti-CD45 (which labels blood cells) and HTO antibodies (BD Biosciences) (Supplementary Table 2) were used together to hashtag and distinguish the different organ Tomato+CD31+ ECs when loaded on the same 10x Genomics port (Extended Data Figs. 6a and 8a). After antibody incubation, samples were washed twice with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged (450g, 5 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. Immediately before FACS analysis, DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added, and the cell suspension was passed slowly through a 70-µm cell strainer attached to a 1-ml syringe for removal of aggregates. Live, DAPI-negative, CD31+CD45− and endogenous-reporter-positive cells were sorted into cold 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes containing 300 µl of sorting buffer. Cells were collected using a 100-µm nozzle at 20 PSI in high-purity mode with a flow rate of fewer than 3,000 events per second to preserve cell viability and minimize contamination. After sorting, cells were pelleted at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C and resuspended in 30–40 µl cell-capture buffer (Ca2+- and Mg2+-free PBS supplemented with 0.04% ultrapure bovine serum albumin; Thermo Fisher, AM2616). Viability and cell concentration were determined using a Countess 3 Automated Cell Counter (Thermo Fisher Scientific) before loading of the 10x Genomics port.

Single-cell suspensions were loaded on to the 10x Genomics Chromium Controller system for encapsulation into emulsion droplets. The 10x Genomics Chromium single-cell 3′ RNA-seq library preparation and sequencing were carried out at the CNIC Genomics Unit according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Each port was loaded with 20,000 to 50,000 cells. Final libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 platform, with software v.1.7.2.

scRNA-seq data were aligned and quality controlled by the CNIC Bioinformatics Unit using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9). Clustering, cell type identification and downstream analysis were performed by I.G.-G. The following pipeline was applied for transcript alignment, quantification, quality control and cell type classification.

Reference transcriptomes were generated using the Ensembl GRCm38 mouse genome, build version 98 (sep2019.archive.ensembl.org). Genes metadata were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. To enable downstream analysis of gene deletion efficiency and soluble versus full-length isoform abundance, we appended Vegfr2 (also known as Kdr) exon 3, Kdr exon 30, Vegfr1 (also known as Flt1) exon 13b and Flt1 exon 30 to the reference transcriptome as custom metadata features. Gene annotations were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. Raw sequencing reads from gene expression libraries, hashtag oligonucleotides and targeted transcript sequences were aligned and quantified using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9).

Downstream analyses were performed using R (v.4.5.0) and the Seurat package (v.5.5.1; https://satijalab.org/seurat/)49. Cells were filtered for removal of low-quality profiles and technical artifacts using the following criteria: 2,000–30,000 total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), 800–6,000 detected genes, mitochondrial transcript content less than 25%, fewer than 65% of reads mapping to the top 50 expressed genes and fewer than 0.1% haemoglobin transcripts. Cells with fewer than 15 hashtag UMIs were excluded to improve sample assignment accuracy. To enrich for endothelial populations and exclude hematopoietic contamination, we also required cells to express Cdh5 (normalized expression greater than 0.1) and no or very low expression of Ptprc (normalized expression less than 0.1). Cells identified as doublets on the basis of hashtag antibody signals were removed. Demultiplexing by organ was performed using sample-specific hashtag oligonucleotide signals (Supplementary Table 2) and after confirmed by organ-specific EC markers, and all downstream analyses were conducted separately for each organ ECs.

Mitochondrial genes, haemoglobin genes and transgenes were removed before clustering to avoid biasing of normalization and dimensionality reduction. Filtered count data were log-normalized and scaled before analysis. Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis, and batch effects across independent ports were corrected with the Harmony algorithm50.

We clustered cells by constructing a shared nearest neighbour graph and applying the Louvain community detection algorithm to identify distinct cell populations. The optimal number of principal components for dimensionality reduction was determined using an elbow plot, and clustering resolution parameters were selected on the basis of the EC complexity observed in each organ.

Clusters and cells were classified using the SingleR function from the SingleR package v.2.10.0 (ref. 51). Putative doublets were identified as cell clusters that had high total UMI or gene counts or unusual gene coexpression or were located in principal component analysis outliers. Cells classified as singlets were retained and reclustered. Final cluster identities were manually curated on the basis of known EC subtypes and literature-based markers. The FUNCTION_Dotplot_Markers custom function in R was used to find and plot top marker genes per cluster to determine cell identities.

To assess the rate of exon deletion in Vegfr2flox/flox samples, we computed the number of UMI reads aligned to each exon, including the floxed region and the terminal 3′ exon or untranslated region (which is typically overrepresented in 10x Genomics 3′ libraries). Only reads with valid barcodes, UMIs and matching strand orientation were retained.

Read counts for floxed exons were normalized to total UMI counts per cell. These values were added to the Seurat metadata. Deletion efficiency was visualized using dot plots and violin plots, comparing expression of the whole transcript (including the 3′ untranslated region). These visualizations were generated using the custom R function FUNCTION_violin_dotplot_deletion_FC.R, which combines violin plots of single-cell expression distributions with dot plots displaying total average expression numbers and signed fold change between conditions.

To obtain the ratio between the soluble (sVegfr1) and full-length (flVegfr1) isoforms, the normalized reads from exon 13b (the last exon in the soluble form) were divided by the normalized reads of exon 30 (the last exon in the full-length version).

We quantified differences in cell type composition between control and mutant samples for each organ by comparing relative proportions across conditions. For UMAP visualizations (both split and integrated), equal downsampling of the two conditions was performed to ensure identical cell numbers, thereby avoiding sampling bias in visual comparisons.

Differential gene expression between conditions was visualized using volcano plots. These were generated using R functions (FUNCTION_VolcanoPlot) developed in-house that built on the EnhancedVolcano package (v.1.26.0)52. For volcano plots and heatmaps, statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. GSEA was performed using FGSEA with a custom wrapper function (FUNCTION_Fgsea_TableFgsea) based on the FGSEA package. For hallmark pathways, statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea v.1.34.2)53 and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple testing.

Genes used for differential gene expression analysis were prefiltered using FUNCTION_FilterLowExpressionGenes_onlyTable; this removes genes with low and highly heterogeneous expression patterns across cells, which are often inconsistently detected between datasets and potentially reflect technical artefacts such as ambient RNA contamination. The function acts as an empirical, distribution-based filter to improve robustness of downstream differential expression analysis. Differential expression heatmaps were generated using a custom function (FUNCTION_Find_PlotGenesHeatmap_FC_Metadata), implemented in-house and based on the pheatmap package.

Most numerical data shown in charts were first compiled and processed with Microsoft Excel 2019 and 2024 and then analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism v.10.1.0. All bar graphs show mean ± s.d. Experiments were repeated with independent animals, as stated in the source data file or figure legends. Comparisons between two sample groups with a Gaussian distribution were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. Comparisons among more than two groups were made by one-way or two-way analysis of variance followed by multiple comparison tests. Data points were analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining. For mosaic analysis, only samples with less than 50% recombination were selected. The sample sizes were chosen according to the observed statistical variation and published protocols.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

RNA-seq data can be viewed at the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE331295. Unprocessed FACS raw data files and original microscopy images of the data are available upon request. All other data supporting the findings in this study are included in the main article and associated files. Source data are provided with this paper.
