A familiar feeling after last season. Newcastle concede a last kick of the game penalty. Should have held on for the win. It was a soft penalty, Hall dangled out a knee rather than a leg and Munoz made sure he ran into it. But as soon as it's given on the field never going to be…

The points are shared, and Lewis Hall has his hands on his knees. Jaissle protests with the officials. This was a stirring home performance from Newcastle which should build confidence for the season ahead. An irrepressible showing from Wissa was the biggest positive. Iraola will be pleased to get back on the coach with a draw after what was quite a ragged Liverpool performance, their midfield balance looked off.

What a magnificent penalty from Szoboszlai, Hornicek had no chance, and Liverpool have surely snatched a point.

Dominik Szoboszlai equalises from the spot in the 99th minute! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/0Ag9WitqHt

What theatre that would be... Gakpo has the ball in his hands. But no, it’s going to be Szoboszlai.

With the last kick of the game, practically. Kerkez launched the ball forward, Van Dijk competed for a header, Munoz pounced on the seconds, and his pace carried enough threat to prompt Hall to step across the winger and make contact with his knee.

#NEWLIV – 90+6' The referee's call of penalty for the challenge by Hall on Muñoz was checked and confirmed by VAR. REF: "He doesn't play the ball. He makes clear contact". VAR: "It's knee into thigh contact. Confirming the on-field decision of penalty".

So, so poor from Frimpong who hesitates to put a cross in, takes a couple of unconvincing touches, and then commits a foul. Mac Allister. Wissa receives a standing ovation, replaced by Schar.

Gakpo runs down a blind alley, and it is another blunt Liverpool attack. Time running out for them now.

Liverpool corner, won by Lewis Koumas who lacked support but his cross deflects behind.

Hornicek palms away Szoboszlai’s delivery. This has been strong Premier League debut from the goalkeeper.

Newcastle have a throw deep in Liverpool territory after more good work from Wissa, and chaotic defending from Liverpool. Atwell has booked Gakpo for an earlier foul on Wissa.

There will be FIVE minutes of added time.

Murphy with another wonderful cross through the Liverpool six-yard box, but no player in black and white was gambling for a tap in. Liverpool just about still in with a sniff.

Cheers at St James’ Park as Thiaw ushers the ball behind as Kerkez tried to get in behind. Then Frimpong’s touch lets him down, not for the first time.

An aimless cross from Liverpool, and Munoz is penalised at the back post for a push. Liverpool have lacked clarity and intelligence in the last third today, but there is still time.

Big save by Alisson! He narrows the angle to deny Wissa the goal his performance deserves. How important could that prove to be? Liverpool have the ball again.

Liverpool with a long spell of possession in the final third, trying to tire Newcastle legs, but Frimpong’s cross is a little too high for Isak to generate any power with the header. Newcastle are just starting to sit in a touch.

Munoz runs down a blind alley, more sound defending from Lewis Hall and the Newcastle players can see the finish line now. They will be only too aware of how they lost this game in the last minute 12 months ago, though.

Szoboszlai shoots against the well, and the Araujo is booked for bundling over a Newcastle defender. Wissa thought he was away for Newcastle but the flag goes up for offside.

Frimpong does well to keep things alive for Liverpool, and there are half-hearted appeals for a handball penalty but Thiaw was down by his side. Another Liverpool sub: Lewis Koumas is on for Gravenberch.

The long throw is headed away, but Murphy catches Mac Allister and Liverpool have a free-kick in a crossing position. Though you never can tell with Szoboszlai around.

Here come those changes from Newcastle: Murphy and Bamba on for Elanga and Miley. Hall’s delivery from the free-kick won by Wissa was poor.

Liverpool have Newcastle penned in, but Munoz’s pass is overhit and Newcastle have a goal kick. Jaissle is about to introduce Jacob Murphy from the bench. Wissa, Newcastle’s best player by a stretch, does well to win a free-kick high up the pitch from Szoboszlai.

Araujo is on for Jacquet at the back for Liverpool, who have just threatened again. Szoboszlai hacked down but the referee waved play on, and Kerkez could not get enough curl on his cross or else Isak would have had a free header.

Willock lifts in a teasing cross from the right, Alisson palms the ball back into danger, and Ramsey cracks a shot wide of the post. Hard to say whether this game is going 3-1 or 2-2 but the scoring is surely not over.

Was that Isak’s moment? Gakpo rolls the ball back to Isak in a good shooting position just inside the box, but he slices his left-footed effort well over the bar. More cheers from the Newcastle fans.

Newcastle really should have three! Defence-splitting pass from Miley to release Hall, who feeds a teasing cross into the six-yard box, but Wissa could only get studs on it. Better connection and that was a goal. Liverpool so fragile at the back, though.

Stuart Atwell has been guessing on decisions throughout this game, and Jacob Ramsey has just been booked for what looked a clean challenge on Isak, who produced a lovely turn initially. Newcastle survive the free-kick.

But then Gakpo has acres of space to run into, but Botman saves the day in the box. The game is haywire at the moment.

Here come the Liverpool changes: Ngumoha, who was the match-winner last season here, Wirtz are the players off, replaced by Munoz and Mac Allister.

Liverpool will be kicking themselves, they had Newcastle on the ropes. Iraola is preparing a triple sub. Willock was the goalscorer, but it was also a brilliant assist from Wissa.

The equaliser had been coming but that was really poor from a defensive perspective as everyone backed off Cody Gakpo and let him pick his spot.

You also have to question the decision to keep Will Osula on. He was obviously struggling to move freely and it has meant Newcastle did not have an out ball.

But, just as I was going to be critical of manager Matthias Jassile one of his substitutes puts Newcastle back in front and it a brilliant goal. Magnificent build up play from Wissa, who skipped away from three Liverpool players, but it is even better from Joe Willock who takes the pass in his stride, shows great skill t o take it on jis stride and away from Frimpong and the finish is sublime, curled into the bottom corner.

Jaissle can claim that as a magical substitution, but it is superb individual goal from Joe Willock. Another Newcastle counter-attack, Wissa does brilliantly to wriggle away from three players in midfield, and Willock dribbles inside Frimpong before arcing a shot into the far corner. Outstanding finish.

"Wow!"Joe Willock restores Newcastle's advantage almost instantly with an exceptional finish! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/8IKPUgqapK

Jaissle with a double sub immediately after conceding: Joe Willock and Jacob Ramsey are on, replacing William Osula and Sean Steur who was a little slack on the Gakpo goal.

The game is one-way traffic, Liverpool looking to turn the screw.

The man linked with a move to Spurs all summer has equalised for Liverpool. He had a sighter a few minutes earlier, and it was too easy for Gakpo to receive the ball behind Newcastle’s midfield, and he had time to pick out the far corner with a clean hit from outside the box. Game on.

Cody Gakpo with a fine finish to equalise for Liverpool! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/cfDQWbES2v

Just two touches inside the Newcastle penalty area from Isak so far, he has been subdued. Nice idea from Gakpo, chopping inside from the left, and curling a shot not far wide of the top corner.

Good defending from Lewis Hall up against Ngumoha, before Van Dijk passes the ball straight of play. Wissa wanted a free-kick for a challenge from behind by Gravenberch but the referee judged he touched the ball first.

Scramble at the back post from the Liverpool corner, but then a loose touch from Wirtz prompts a Newcastle break and there was a chance for Elanga to dribble into the box but he put the breaks on.

The game is already really stretched, holes appearing in Liverpool’s midfield. Wissa’s poked through ball towards Osula was just a tad overhit.

Liverpool have made a sharp start from kick off, winning a corner.

Just because it is a manager’s first game, we shouldn’t pull our punches. That was a scandalous first half performance from Liverpool and there is absolutely no difference in watching them now compared to what they offered through much of last season. Maybe the disappointment wasn’t about the man in the dugout. Maybe it was about the players wearing the Red shirt.

5 & 18 - 5 - Liverpool have conceded in the opening five minutes on MD1 of a Premier League season for the very first time.The Reds are winless in 18 Premier League away games when falling 1-0 behind (D6 L12) since beating Crystal Palace 2-1 in December 2023.Baptism. pic.twitter.com/K1HF2wNRVP

Newcastle will be delighted to go in leading the game at half time but there were some worrying signs before the break.

They had stopped getting up the pitch and were invited a lot of pressure from Liverpool. Will Osula has clearly picked up an injury – he took a whack on his achilles midway through the half – and will surely need to be replaced by Nick Woltemade in the second half with Yoane Wissa moving up top.

Alexander Isak has been on the receiving end of a number of heavy tackles and has looked pretty miserable so far on his return to St James’ Park.

But Liverpool are not going to keep getting into dangerous positions and fail to capitalise on them. Things for Matthias Jaissle to sort out before the second half.

LFC Midfield all bombing forward happened all pre season, madness!

Plenty of possession for Liverpool, but not enough cutting edge of crispness in their play in the final third. On top of that problem, they were vulnerable to Newcastle’s pace and direct play early on although that threat abated as the half progressed. Jaissle will be delighted with the commitment and application of his players, but Osula may have to come off with a knock.

Isak hooks a pass towards Frimpong straight out of play, causing much mirth among the home fans.

Foul given against Wissa on Gravenberch, and the Newcastle forward needs to be careful on a yellow. I’m not sure there was any contact at all. Wissa drags a shot across the face of Liverpool’s goal and wide.

Gravenberch with a speculative shot which is blocked, before Dedic blasts the ball off Gakpo to win a goal kick. Dan Burn is watching on from the stands, Newcastle’s new club captain who is absent because of a rolled ankle. Also up there in the gods is England manager Thomas Tuchel.

Much better cross from Frimpong, but Dedic clears at the back post for a Liverpool corner. Danger as Gakpo flicks the ball on at the neat post, and the ball bounces off Botman and behind for another corner. Gravenberch tries a cute reverse pass towards Isak, but it deflects through to Hornicek. Isak has been ever so quiet.

William Osula is hobbling up top for Newcastle, which is a worry because has been a menace so far. The same can be said of Yoane Wissa who is having a stormer as a second striker, dropping into midfield at times.

Stuart Atwell being a little card happy, now Lewis Miley is shown a yellow for a foul on Gravenberch. Just looked a regulation midfield foul, not sure a booking was necessary.

Osula took the free-kick, straight into the wall, but his follow up effort deflects off Szoboszlai and behind for a corner. Excellent delivery from Lewis Hall, cleared by Van Dijk.

Wirtz and Isak do well down the left to start a Liverpool counter with runners forward, but Frimpong’s delivery from the right is atrocious.

Liverpool starting to monopolise possession, without a crafty final pass. Kerkez has been booked for holding Elanga, who is giving him a going over on Newcastle’s right flank.

Then Barnes rolls inside Frimpong and drives inside, and the Liverpool right-back is booked for a challenge from behind. May well have been a harsh call, both plays were grasping for a piece of shirt.

Both of Liverpool’s full-backs on yellows now.

Wissa booked for a mistimed challenge, and Liverpool have a free-kick 30 yards out. Szoboszlai is thinking about a shot... but he blasts his shot straight into the wall.

Osula then does very well to make it stick and drag Newcastle up the pitch but the move fizzles out.

It’s an experience in itself watching Andoni Iraola on the sideline. He’s going to have clocked up 10,000 steps for sure by the final whistle and his increasing animation is indicative of Liverpool’s anaemic start. You would expect Liverpool to score at some point but this is a team that has lots of questions to answer.

Isak down on the turf after a strong challenge by Lewis Hall, no foul given much to the delight of the Newcastle fans.

Then the home team cut through Liverpool again, Wissa with a glorious outside of the foot pass behind Jacquet for the run of Osula, but the Liverpool defender just about got a toe to the ball as the striker closed in on Alisson. Great challenge in the end from the wrong side.

Nice counter-movement between Elanga and Dedic the right-back. Elanga faked to drop inside, taking Kerkez and Gakpo with him, and Miley’s switch found Dedic on the outside. Cross is blocked, and Newcastle have a corner. Cleared, and then a poor Szoboszlai pass is blocked when there was a chance to release Wirtz on the counter.

It feels like all the 50:50s are dropping Newcastle’s way at the moment. It has been a very energetic start, the question is whether that is sustainable across the game so early in the season. The tempo will surely drop at some point.

Peter Beardsley, Tino Asprilla and Shaka Hislop among Keegan’s former players watching on.

Hornicek with his first big save of the game, tipping Wirtz’s shot around the post. Newcastle failed to deal with a Kerkez cross and the ball dropped to the German for a snap shot. Newcastle defend the corner.

“There’s only one greedy b-----d,” is the chant from the Newcastle fans (aimed at Isak, for the uninitiated).

Wissa goes down looking for a foul but nothing doing, but there are cheers from the home fans as Isak is beaten to a header and then Sean Steur turns away from pressure well in midfield. There is more bite about the home team in the challenges than Liverpool, Jaissle will be delighted with this.

Echoes of last season with Liverpool’s defence looking suspect against direct play, Alisson with an unconvincing intervention outside his penalty area after the ball held up. He is fortunate that Wissa did not connect with the volley when there was a chance to lob the goalkeeper.

What a difference a year makes. Anthony Elanga was played in on goal against Aston Villa on his Premier League debut for Newcastle United 12 months ago. He looked nervous and hit a tame effort too close to the goalkeeper.

It is fair to say that was a sign of things to come for the winger who endured a miserable first season on Tyneside following a high-profile £55m move from Nottingham Forest. He looked drained of confidence and lacked the composure and technical ability to succeed in black and white stripes.

Fast forward 12 months and he has just taken a very similar chance against Liverpool. The speed of Will Osula sent the visiting defence into retreat, and his pace and excellent first touch set up the chance, which he finished clinically.

That was the player Eddie Howe thought he was signing last summer. It was the player Newcastle supporters thought was going to offer a major upgrade in the right wing position.

If Elanga has a better season this time around it will be a huge boost to new manager Matthias Jaissle.

Elanga vs Kerkez is a match-up which looks advantageous for Newcastle, the Liverpool left-back is at full tilt to get back and by a foul after a lofted Wissa pass over his head towards the rapid Sweden winger.

This is a very open game already, and Liverpool are back on the front foot. Szoboszlai whips in a free-kick which appears to glance of Van Dijk’s head, but the referee awards a corner. Hall clears, but Newcastle do not clear their lines and Gakpo’s shot is blocked by Thiaw.

Liverpool caught out on the break, but it is a really well-executed goal from Newcastle’s perspective. Gravenberch should have let fly at the other end, but after the move broke down Osula was able to receive in space and turn to face Van Dijk and Jacquet. He waited for the support of Elanga to arrive, and he burned down the outside of Kerkez. Well-weighted pass put him through, and the finish across Alisson was ideal.

An electric start! Anthony Elanga gives Newcastle the lead inside 5 minutes! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/8DYYFJ9i6F

Lewis Hall wins a challenge at the edge of the box which receives a roar of approval from the crowd, but Liverpool quickly settle into a long spell of possession, with Gravenberch turning away from pressure, but neglecting to shoot.

This already has the feel of a very helter-skelter game. Newcastle won a free-kick inside 20 seconds, clipped into the penalty area but it was claimed by Alisson. Then a Liverpool attack swept from one end to the other with Wirtz’s shot blocked at the edge of the box. This should be tasty.

That roar turns to vociferous boos as Alexander Isak takes the kick-off.

They would have still been clapping until tomorrow if the whistle hadn’t been blown by referee Stuart Attwell to start the game but the flip from adulation for Kevin Keegan to absolute vitriol towards Alexander Isak was incredible. 50,000 in black and white are singing a song aimed at him. The only two words we can get away with printing are “ole, ole!” - use your imagination for what might have preceded it!

A period of applause for Kevin Keegan at St James' Park 👏❤️ pic.twitter.com/AsSGOkpVPN

There is a minute’s applause for Keegan, which ends with a defending roar.

Liverpool have just taken to the field for their warm up, predictably to a back drop of pantomime booing. But there is a nice touch from the club, as each member of Andoni Iraola’s squad is wearing a jersey with “Keegan 7” on the back. It’s going to be a day of heavy emotion.

Alan Shearer was one of those fans holding up a white card:

The Keegan quote on the Newcastle banner is: “I want people to dream about their football club. They should, we should all be dreamers at heart. Some people are the opposite and say ‘we can’t do that’, but when you ask them why, they can’t give a reason. Well, I say, ‘Why not?’”

Banners are being unfurled in the Gallowgate End. Alan Shearer and Stuart Pearce are in the stands, and Les Ferdinand is pitchside speaking on Sky.

As you know it’s a transition phase and a huge challenge. There will be some activity in the transfer market new week, hopefully, but we go for it, we are as ready as we can be. That’s something we want to show the fans, we want to go all in.

As soon as I saw him on the pitch, I was falling in love. He is a great guy with great potential.

I’m not worried. As a manager, a player or a squad, if it is against you you want to play this kind of games.

Difficult call, Jeremy has very good skills with the ball, without the ball they will be very demanding today, playing against Wissa and Osula.

Alexander Isak is going to be in for the sort of hostile afternoon unseen in English football for years.

Not since Michael Owen has a player left Newcastle and been so universally despised. Owen was accused of ducking out of a relegation battle to ensure he secured a lucrative free transfer move after an injury-ravaged spell in the North East.

If anything, Isak was even worse, He went on strike, refusing to play for the club again, despite having three years left on his contract, in order to force a move to Liverpool. It felt like the ultimate betrayal and crossed a line with Geordies. They will love you and worship players as good as Isak, but if you behave like the Sweden international did you become the ultimate villain.

Isak was a superb player in black and white stripes, arguably their best since the takeover by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in 2021. He was top goalscorer two years running and was the focal point of Eddie Hower’s attack as they qualified for the Champions League twice and won the Carabao Cup.

He could have been a Geordie legend, but he left in such an ugly and acrimonious fashion. Isak forced Newcastle to buckle from their not for sale stance, rejecting a pay rise and a new contract, insisting he would never play for the club again even if they refused to sell him, that he will be tarnished forever.

It is sad in many ways and shows the ugly side of the game. I’m told he does regret the manner of his exit, especially his falling out with Howe. They have not spoken since. It has weighed heavily on him since his move to Anfield.

Looks like Rio Ngumoha will play on the right flank with Cody Gakpo left, Wirtz in the No 10 role behind Isak.

Liverpool XI: Alisson; Frimpong, Van Dijk, Jacquet, Kerkez; Gravenberch, Szoboszlai; Ngumoha, Wirtz, Gakpo; Isak

The Reds to take on Newcastle in our season opener ✊ #NEWLIV

Barnes, Wissa, Osula and Elanga start in what could be a front four. Lewis Miley and Sean Steur, just 20 and 18 respectively, will need to get through an immense amount of work in midfield.

Newcastle United XI: Hornicek; Dedic, Thiaw (c), Botman, Hall; Miley, Steur; Elanga, Wissa, Barnes; Osula

Sir Kenny Dalglish and Bobby Moncur are the representatives of both clubs with wreaths, and Shola Ameobi is behind Dalglish. Ian Rush is also in attendance, who spent one season on Tyneside in the twilight of his career when Dalglish was the manager.

There will be a powerful expression of unity between Newcastle United and Liverpool supporters in memory of their shared icon, Kevin Keegan, before this afternoon’s game.

A man who meant so much to both clubs: a phenomenal player for Liverpool and a force of nature who transformed Newcastle as both a player and a manager.

The cooperation between the two to ensure St James’ Park can deliver a special tribute to a remarkable figure in English football has been heartwarming.

The sale of Curtis Jones to Inter Milan means that for the first time since Liverpool came into existence in 1892, the prospect of them going through the season without fielding a player who was born in the city for a game is real. That will surely sting Liverpool fans more than most, given the city’s strong sense of regional identity. You can read more on the subject in this article by Dominic King. Trent on loan in January, anyone?

He has also not sugar-coated anything. Jaissle knows he is up against it. Time is the enemy, given how late he arrived in pre-season and he understands the size of the task ahead.

These are early days, but the energy and purpose he has brought to the job have impressed everyone at all levels of the club. Clear communication is at the heart of everything. He explains what he expects, what he needs and what has to be done, no matter who the conversation is with.

It is fitting that Newcastle United vs Liverpool is a Premier League opening weekend fixture following the death of Kevin Keegan at the age of 75 last month.

All corners of St James’ Park will pay tribute and show their appreciation for the former player and manager who means a great deal to both sets of supporters.

Fans will find a printed message from the Keegan family on the back of black and white cards on their seat, which they will hold up to display a mural before kick-off.

As well as playing for both clubs, Keegan was Newcastle’s manager when they were beaten by a last-gasp Stan Collymore goal at Anfield in April 1996, a 4-3 defeat remembered as one of the great Premier League games.

This fixture usually delivers entertainment, and with new managers Matthias Jaissle and Andoni Iraola promising front-footed, ‘vertical’ football, there should be goals. That was certainly the case last August, when Newcastle fought back from two down with 10 men, before Rio Ngumoha scored a memorable winner.

It has been a summer of tumult for Newcastle, losing manager Eddie Howe, as well as key players Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes. There has been bullish talk of “Newcastle 2.0” from David Hopkinson, the club’s chief executive, and the club believe they have found a promising coach, but fans have understandably revised expectations downwards.

Liverpool are a difficult team to read; champions only 18 months ago but brittle last season, which resulted in Arne Slot’s dismissal. Iraola’s appointment is a shift back towards Jurgen Klopp’s style. That will be music to the ears of Anfield regulars, but holes remain in the squad. Central midfield has not been replenished; they need a Mohamed Salah replacement, and their strength at full-back is questionable. Much will depend on how 21-year-old central defender Jérémy Jacquet fares alongside Vigin van Dijk but he impressed in pre-season.Full team news on the way shortly.

#1622. Arsenal transfer news: Gunners 'targeting' world's most creative teenage defender

By Carter White | 09 Nov 2026 16:18

Arsenal-linked Ryan Augusto has topped an extensive list of football's most creative young full-backs.

Mikel Arteta's side extended their lead at the top of the Premier League standings with a 1-0 success over newly-promoted Hull City on Saturday afternoon, when Martin Odegaard netted the winner in the second half.

The Emirates contest saw the return of winger Christos Tzolis following an injury setback, with Arsenal supposedly eyeing up a move for RB Leipzig and Norway wide attacker Antonio Nusa ahead of the 2027 transfer windows.

The 21-year-old was particularly impressive against Manchester City in the Champions League last week and has also made a sensational start to the Bundesliga term, scoring four goals and providing seven assists across nine appearances.

The Premier League champions were known to be in the market for a high-profile forward player during the most recent summer window, missing out on the signings of Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez.

Always on the lookout for the next big talent, Arsenal were linked to Bragantino defender Augusto last month, with the youngster enjoying a breakthrough campaign in Brazil this calendar year.

Now, the 19-year-old has received a noteworthy accolade, placing top of a study based on creative full-backs and wing-backs under the age of 20 by the CIES Football Observatory, as relayed by Brazilian outlet Trivela.

Over the course of his 12 Brasileiro matches so far in 2026, Augusto has managed to produce 0.32 expected assists per 90 minutes - a figure greater than any of his positional counterparts across 52 top-flight leagues.

This clearly points towards the excellent attacking ability of the right-back, who is likely to secure a switch to a European club in the near future, given his undoubted potential.

Augusto also possesses the qualities to invert into midfield and combine with teammates in the centre of the pitch - a characteristic which would be helpful for Arteta's Premier League holders.

Conceding just five goals in 10 Premier League matches so far this season, Arsenal are undoubtedly the best defensive side in the division, as was the case last campaign when they beat Manchester City to the title.

A major part of that solidity, right-back is a position of riches for the Gunners, who have recently welcomed Jurrien Timber back to first-team action following a significant injury layoff.

There is also good reason to mention the contributions of England international Ben White, with the nonchalant character building an excellent relationship with Bukayo Saka on Arsenal's right-hand side.

#1621. CELTIC 3 BESIKTAS 2: Duran and Osmand make the difference from the bench as O'Neill's men roar back to claim precious victory

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:33 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:56 EST, 5 November 2026

By the time the Celtic players had reacquainted themselves with the concept of a lap of honour on a European night, those who had come to decry the club’s hierarchy had shuffled off into the night.

This somewhat unexpected outcome saved Martin O’Neill from the ignominy of being the first manager in the history of the Parkhead club to suffer five straight losses in European competition.

It should also lower the temperature in the ongoing feud between the directors and the fanbase for a few days at least.

After a diabolical start to their Europa League campaign, O’Neill’s men are belatedly up and running. The task of accruing sufficient points to reach the knock-out round again is still enormous although it is not yet beyond them. There’s life in this yet.

Of the four sides who Celtic were drawn to play in Glasgow in this phase, Besiktas looked the most imposing. In taking their scalp, O’Neill’s side will have received a much-needed infusion of self-belief. An inexorable slide towards a full-blown crisis has been avoided, for now.

This was quite the night. A drab and goalless first half was no indication of what was to come.

Camilo Duran squeezes home the winner in the 87th minute for Celtic

Substitutes Callum Osmand (left) and Camilo Duran turned the tide for Celtic

O’Neill’s men fell behind through a penalty but, to their enormous credit, they did not wilt.

So much of the credit for a famous triumph belonged to two players who, oddly, didn’t start the match.

Callum Osmand levelled with his first touch and was scintillating in everything he did from that point on.

Camilo Duran, another who’d started the night clad in a tracksuit, edged O’Neill’s side in front following a majestic ball from Osmand.

When Besiktas levelled with five minutes remaining, many of the home supporters would probably have settled for a draw. Not a bit of it. Duran’s second of the night, two minutes later, secured a magnificent victory, one which might just prove to be a turning point.

For those arriving in the stadium and checking their phones, O’Neill’s team selection required a second take. After playing just 31 minutes across three substitute appearances, Jordan Lotomba was handed his first start at right back ahead of Colby Donovan.

James Forrest and Sebastian Tounekti were deployed on the flanks with Kasper Hogh selected in place of Duran at centre-forward. So much for a must-win game.

There was familiarity in the Besiktas side in the shape of former Rangers winger Vaclav Cerny and Oh Hyeon-gyu, formerly a striker in this parish.

Although the Turks controlled the first half, Celtic did fashion the first real opening. Mika Baur fed Tounekti who squared the ball to Benjamin Nygren. The Swede ought to have done much better than fire wildly over.

Celtic’s attempt to press high was admirable. All too often, though, the men in black just played through it.

Forrest did well to move the ball on and invited Lotomba to attack it. He was easily brushed aside.

Duran celebrates making it 2-1 in a thrilling second half at Parkhead

It became a recurring theme. Not only were Besiktas technically superior to Celtic in the opening half, collectively, they were physically stronger. If there was a 50/50 to be won, invariably, they won it.

The upshot was that O’Neill’s men made little headway when they got into promising positions.

It said much that the biggest roar of the first half from the home supporters came when Liam Scales took ball then man – that man being Cerny.

You had to wonder what instructions Sam Johnstone had been given. His tactic of launching the ball long to Hogh was, to say the least, optimistic. With next to nothing coming from the flanks, the Dane was again starved of service.

The encouraging thing for O’Neill at the break was the fact that Besiktas’ possession hadn’t translated into too many chances. Cerny fired over. Leandro Trossard forced Johnstone into a good stop, although the offside flag had been raised.

Tounekti contributed another uninspiring display. Time and again, he gathered the ball on the flank. If there was an easy option to take, he took it.

The Tunisian had a chance to play Forrest in after creeping infield. Remarkably, he managed to stumble on the ball and Besiktas sprang another attack.

Although Celtic were level at the break, they’d been feckless. A chance to fashion something from a free-kick saw Tounekti pick out Nygren. The Swede completely lost his footing and the chance was gone.

Callum McGregor was the most relieved man in the ground in the opening seconds of the second period. He turned into trouble on the edge of his own box in the shape of Junior Olaitan and watched as Trossard’s curler flew just over.

Another old head in Forrest came close at the other end, his slalom from right to centre ending with a low shot which the keeper fielded.

Lotomba’s display throughout was poor, entirely in keeping with a player with so little football under his belt.

Osmand made an instant impact in rifling home for 1-1 from the edge of the box

It was no surprise that the error which led to Besiktas’ opener came from him. Johnstone created the initial problem by needlessly smashing a clearance off the frame of Trossard. It broke kindly to Ernest Poku. With no need to panic, Lotomba did exactly that. His scything of his opponent was a clear penalty.

Johnstone stood up to block Olaitan’s initial effort but couldn’t recover in time. The Besiktas man smashed home the rebound once the ball had fallen from the night sky. It was scarcely ill-deserved at that point.

O’Neill threw on Duran, Osmand and Donovan. The changes yielded an immediate return.

Advanced on the left of the box, McGregor showed composure to square the ball to Osmand. Any fears of ring-rust from the substitute were misplaced. A crisp right-foot shot flew into the bottom corner to level.

Credit where it’s due. Having hardly worried the Turks up to that stage, Celtic found something. Scales had his head in his hands after being denied a headed goal from a corner by a smart save by Alexander Nobel in the Besiktas goal.

With Osmand’s work rate giving the home fans something to get behind, Celtic improved. Another surge by the forward brought Hogh into the game. Duran’s pace took him into a dangerous position but the Dane couldn’t find him.

Osmand then fed the advanced Nygren. Again, the normally dependable Swede didn’t have his shooting boots on.

The former Fulham player seemed to be everywhere. It was his brilliantly measured pass which cut the Turkish defence wide open as Celtic turned the game on its head with 78 minutes remaining.

Perfectly weighted and angled, it still asked a lot of Duran. The Colombian did brilliantly, gathering and rounding the keeper in the blink of an eye then rolling the ball into an empty net.

As Celtic Park rejoiced, substitute Haissem Hassan fizzed one into the keeper’s arms.

How O’Neill’s men would come to rue that moment. There didn’t appear to be much on when substitute Orkun Kokcu took aim 25 yards out and thundered the ball low past Johnstone.

A slow burner of a game had certainly sprang into life. And we weren’t done yet.

Celtic dusted themselves down and came again. Donovan motored across the field and found Tierney. The full-back’s strike didn’t have the power to trouble the keeper but fell kindly for Duran. At the second attempt, he bundled the ball home.

#1620. Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age1,2,3. How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested4, with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts5,6,7,8. Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

Europe’s present-day linguistic landscape is dominated by Romance, Germanic and Slavic languages, which expanded relatively recently during the Iron Age10,11,12,13. Before these events, Celtic languages were prominent across Europe1,2,3: Lepontic has been documented in northwestern Italy (2600–2100 bp), Celtiberian in central-northeastern Iberia (2200–1900 bp) and Gaulish across present-day France, central Europe, northern Italy and the Balkans (2500–1400 bp)14,15 (Fig. 1a). In the modern era, Celtic languages have retreated to the northwestern Atlantic fringe, where they persist as two groups: the Goidelic languages Irish, Manx and Scottish Gaelic; and the Brittonic languages Welsh, Cornish and Breton.

a, The four proposed source regions for the spread of the Celtic languages (circled) and the approximate pre-Roman and premodern distribution of Celtic languages from roughly 2000 bp (shaded). b, Tree schematic illustrating the position of Proto-Celtic relative to events that bound its emergence: the divergence of its predecessor (Pre-Celtic) from other Indo-European branches and the subsequent divergence into Brittonic and Goidelic (Insular Celtic). The tree structure and branch lengths are shown for illustrative purposes only and remain unresolved. c, Density plot showing the overlap of estimates for the divergence of Pre-Celtic (computational, quantitative), the emergence and dissolution of Proto-Celtic (archaeological and linguistic, qualitative) and the subsequent divergence of Goidelic and Brittonic (computational, quantitative). The linguistic studies from which the estimates come are depicted in Extended Data Fig. 1 and detailed in Supplementary Table 5.1. d,e, Geographical (d) and temporal (e) distributions of ancient samples included in the dataset that overlap with the region and timelines from a and c. In d, a small amount of jitter is added to the geographical coordinates. C. E., central-eastern; N., northern; S., southern; W., western. Base maps in a and d were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

All Celtic languages diverged from an undocumented ancestral language, Proto-Celtic (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a). This language is defined by a series of linguistic innovations present in all Celtic languages, but absent from the other Indo-European languages, including closely related Italic and Lusitanian (Supplementary Note 5). Whereas there is widespread agreement that Indo-European dialects, including the one ancestral to Proto-Celtic, spread across Europe from the Pontic Steppe after 5000 bp (refs. 16,17,18,19), the centre and timing of the subsequent dispersal of Celtic within Europe remain contentious4. Existing hypotheses generally fall within one of the following four models:

The Bell Beaker model associates the Celtic split and dispersal with the Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age Bell Beaker Complex (roughly 4750–4500 to 4000–3800 bp)20,21,22,23, which spanned much of western and central Europe. Under this model, Celtic diverged largely in situ over the millennia following the Bell Beaker expansion. By contrast, the following three models place the formation of Proto-Celtic after 4000 bp.

The Celtic-from-the-West model (Fig. 1a) claims that Proto-Celtic emerged from relatively undiversified Indo-European dialects within long-distance maritime networks of the Atlantic Bronze Age Culture (3300–2700 bp)24, connecting Atlantic Iberia, parts of France, Ireland and Britain. It further posits a subsequent eastward expansion of a Gaulish–Brittonic–Goidelic Celtic subgroup into central Europe during the Hallstatt C period (2750–2600 bp), traced archaeologically through the distribution of Gündlingen swords25.

The Celtic-from-the-Centre model, in turn, posits that Proto-Celtic emerged neither along the Atlantic seaboard nor from eastern central Europe (next model). Instead, it situates this ancestral language in inland France and possibly northwestern Italy 4000–3000 bp, with a subsequent spread in many directions, including to Britain, Italy and Spain, after 3000 bp (refs. 26,27,28) (Fig. 1a). This model rejects overly strong archaeological–linguistic correlations and is instead supported by a relative density of Celtic toponyms and personal names in France.

Finally, the longstanding Celtic-from-the-East model places the formation of Proto-Celtic in eastern central Europe (Fig. 1a) and associates its diversification with the Late Bronze Age Urnfield Culture29,30, the subsequent Hallstatt Culture and La Tène archaeological horizon5,6,7,8, or a combination of these. The documentation of Lepontic Celtic inscriptions in the Urnfield-derived Alpine Golasecca Culture (2850–2350 bp) has been taken to support this model30. In addition, under this model (as well as models (2) and (3)), the geographic distribution of the Iron Age La Tène Culture, extending from France to the Balkans, broadly coincides with the distribution of Gaulish and closely related Celtic dialects31.

These models differ in their proposed centres and chronologies for the formation and spread of Celtic and imply conflicting proposals of human mobility. We therefore test to what degree each model is supported by past population genomic data, similar to approaches that have proved to be illuminative in other historical-linguistic debates11,12,16,17,32,33,34,35. We note, in this context, that the terms ‘spread’ and ‘population movements’ are used as purely descriptive terms that do not speak to the social mechanism driving them.

We expand on the results of a parallel study on the Germanic languages32, leveraging a filtered dataset of 4,587 imputed ancient human genomes that temporally and geographically encompasses the regions in which early Celtic languages have been historically documented (Fig. 1d,e and Supplementary Table 1.1). In addition, we assembled an auxiliary dataset including individuals from Urnfield contexts in Iberia, Celtic-associated contexts in Britain and southwest Germany, and Bronze Age northern Italy (Supplementary Table 1.4). We used identity-by-descent (IBD) mixture modelling and qpAdm, as well as an updated version of chromopainter together with Sourcefind (Methods), to distinguish population continuity from directional gene flow and to test whether proposed linguistic dispersals require additional, unsupported demographic events.

Current evidence suggests that the Indo-European dialect ancestral to the Celtic languages entered Europe along with a ‘massive migration’ from the Pontic Steppe16,17. In western Europe, the earliest Steppe ancestry appears in people of the Bell Beaker Complex36, whose cultural package in northwestern Europe includes Maritime Beaker influence from Iberia, and All-Over-Corded and All-Over-Ornamented Beaker influence from the Corded Ware region to the east37. Western and eastern contributions are also represented genetically, with Bell Beaker individuals deriving ancestry in various proportions from western Neolithic and eastern Steppe sources. To test whether their Steppe ancestry persisted in the four proposed formative regions for Proto-Celtic, we performed IBD mixture modelling (Methods). In brief, a palette is created for every ancient individual in the dataset, representing the proportion of IBD segments of DNA shared with all 386 clusters in the dataset. The palette of each ‘target’ individual is then modelled as the best-fitting combination of the palettes of the ‘source’ groups, using non-negative least squares in the R package limSolve (v.1.5.6)38. Full IBD mixture modelling results, including source-set definitions, spatial and temporal distributions, alternative source models and sensitivity analyses, are provided in Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Figs. 1.1–1.58 and Supplementary Tables 1.1–1.6.

As sources, we included groups of individuals from Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related contexts, together with a series of earlier source groups (Supplementary Figs. 1.1 and 1.2 and Supplementary Note 1). For source individuals, we prioritized early Bell Beaker and Corded Ware individuals to measure the persistence of their ancestry through time. We also prioritized individuals with high Steppe ancestry and minimal Neolithic Farmer ancestries as sources, to allow more Farmer ancestry in later individuals to be detected. As we are interested specifically in the spread of Steppe ancestry, we refer to these ancestry sources as Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related ancestry, while acknowledging that many Neolithic-related sources also contributed to Corded Ware and Bell Beaker populations32,39. When including a single, early Steppe source (Yamnaya-related), we find Steppe ancestry appearing in eastern and northern Europe between 5000 bp and 4500 bp (Supplementary Fig. 1.31a), spreading to western and southern Europe between 4500 bp and 4000 bp, consistent with expectations16,17,39. When including the two other sources with high Steppe ancestry (Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related, Extended Data Fig. 2c), we find that Steppe ancestry of individuals in the Corded Ware region of northern and eastern Europe is now modelled with Corded Ware-related ancestry (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 1.31b). In the Bell Beaker region of western, central and southern Europe between 4500 bp and 4000 bp, we find the Steppe ancestry of individuals modelled as Bell Beaker-related (Fig. 2), as previously demonstrated32. These ancestries remain dominant in the respective regions through to the Iron Age (Fig. 2). We note an influx of Corded Ware-related ancestry 4000–3600 bp in people of the Únětice Culture in central Europe (Extended Data Fig. 3), consistent with expectations40. However, we find that Únětice people genetically contribute little to no ancestry to later people in the region, or to Celtic-speaking regions more broadly (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1.52). The absence of an influx of Corded Ware-related ancestry from northern Europe or further Yamnaya-related ancestry from eastern Europe, together with the persistence of Bell Beaker-related ancestry, is consistent with a Bell Beaker-mediated entry of the dialects ancestral to Indo-European languages spoken in the region during the Iron Age, including Celtic, and is thus key to evaluating all four models.

The size and fullness of the moons represent the proportion of each ancestry modelled. Whereas only a subset of sources is shown here, the results can be seen for all ancestries as timelines in Supplementary Fig. 1.15 and in ‘ADMIXTURE’ style plots in Supplementary Fig. 1.6. Base maps were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

Next, we look to the region in which Steppe ancestry was incorporated during the formation of Bell Beaker-related populations. Across the Bell Beaker range, we find individuals with the highest proportions of Steppe ancestry to the northwest and lower proportions to the south, suggestive of a more northern origin (Supplementary Fig. 1.31a). When using the Bell Beaker-related source, we find that most individuals in Britain, Ireland, France and the Netherlands have higher proportions of Bell Beaker-related ancestry than in central Europe (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1.41). This pattern remains even when using alternative Bell Beaker and Corded Ware sources from the Czech Republic (Supplementary Figs. 1.40 and 1.42). The expansion to Britain and Ireland from northwestern mainland Europe is also consistent with a previous study indicating that the Bell Beakers of the Lower Rhine formed through a mixture of Corded Ware and local Rhine–Meuse Neolithic ancestry, before spreading to Britain41. Our results indicate that this expansion also reached central and southern Europe. The linguistic identity of Bell Beaker groups cannot be directly inferred from genomic evidence. However, if Indo-European dialects were introduced to the region by this expansion, as previously proposed, it provides a potential vector for the Indo-European dialect ancestral to Celtic. Further sampling from northern France to Germany will help refine this northwestern region.

Over a millennium separates the presumed arrival of Indo-European language varieties in western Europe (roughly 4300 bp) from Iron Age Celtic-speaking populations (roughly 2500 bp) (Fig. 1a). Although northwestern Bell Beaker-related ancestry persisted, the extent to which the population structure within this region changed remains unclear. Evaluating the four models on Celtic origins therefore requires reconstructing the demographic processes that affected Bell Beaker-derived groups after roughly 4000 bp.

Detecting the movement of people during this time has so far proved difficult, due to the close genetic relation between all individuals postdating the arrival of Steppe ancestry. Here we apply two complementary approaches. First, we refine Farmer ancestry as a proxy for mobility by identifying the specific source region of European Farmer ancestry (set C3). This is informative about where the initial admixture occurred, allowing us to infer the region from which later movements spread. Second, we model the later movements directly, using Bronze Age sources from the southeastern and southwestern ends of the region in which Bell Beaker ancestry spread (set C4). The movement from a specific region should be reflected in both the Neolithic Farmer proxy and the Bronze Age source. Rather than attempting to pinpoint specific source populations, these proxies represent broader regional ancestries, allowing the likely spatiotemporal range of possible source populations to be inferred.

To identify variation in the specific sources of Farmer-related ancestry across the Bell Beaker region, we performed IBD mixture modelling (Supplementary Note 1). We included source individuals from IBD clusters associated with Neolithic Britain and Ireland (British–Irish Neo.-related), France and Iberia (Iberia–France Neo.-related), Italy (Italy Neo.-related) and the Czech Republic (Euro. Neo.-related), encompassing the proposed homelands for Celtic. In addition, we included a series of Neolithic-related groups, Bronze Age Anatolia (Anatolia BA-related), Polish Globular Amphora Culture (GAC-related) and Early Anatolian Farmers (E. Anatolia-related). The geographical distribution of these Neolithic-related clusters is plotted in Extended Data Fig. 2b. For the ancestries persisting after roughly 4000 bp (Supplementary Fig. 1.16), we performed spatiotemporal kriging to identify the regions in which these ancestries are found at the end of the Bell Beaker period. We find British–Irish Neo.-related ancestry in Britain and Ireland, Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry in southern France and Iberia, Italy Neo.-related ancestry around the Adriatic and Anatolia BA-related ancestry in the Balkans (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4). We confirmed the spatiotemporal results by plotting the raw results (Supplementary Fig. 1.32).

a, Spatiotemporal kriging results from roughly 4400 bp, showing regions with distinct Neolithic-related ancestry around the time of arrival of Steppe ancestry. Brighter colours indicate a higher proportion of ancestry modelled. Values falling exactly on bin boundaries are included in the lower bin. Kriging was performed on the IBD mixture modelling set C3 results. The raw mixture modelling results for these ancestries can be visualized in Supplementary Fig. 1.32. Kriging results at roughly 4800 bp, 4400 bp, 3300 bp and 2600 bp are also shown in Extended Data Fig. 4. b, IBD mixture modelling results for England, France and the Czech Republic during the Bronze and Iron Ages, highlighting the changes in Neolithic-related ancestries from 4800 bp to 2000 bp. For each target individual (n = 588), point estimates of the proportions of ancestry modelled from these ancestry sources are plotted. For each point estimate, standard errors were calculated using a weighted block jackknife with n = 22 chromosomes, sequentially leaving out one chromosome at a time. The trendline shows the rolling median of the point estimates, using a window of 5. Base maps in a were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

To model movements more directly, we included Bronze Age source individuals from around 4000 bp, a point in time that marks the end of the Bell Beaker period and predates almost all linguistic and archaeological estimates for the formation of Proto-Celtic (Extended Data Fig. 1). From southwestern Europe, we included individuals from Bronze Age southern France–northern Iberia (S. France–N. Iberia BA-related, Extended Data Fig. 2d), where Bell Beaker-related and the local Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestries are found (Figs. 2 and 3a). From southeastern Europe, where Bell Beaker-related, Italy Neo.-related and Anatolia BA-related ancestries are found (Figs. 2 and 3a), we included individuals from Bronze Age Hungary and Serbia (Hungary–Serbia BA-related, Extended Data Fig. 2d). On the basis of spatiotemporal kriging and plotting the raw mixture modelling proportions, we find these ancestries restricted to southwestern and southeastern Europe roughly 4000 bp (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 5).

a, Spatiotemporal kriging results showing the regions in which S. France–N. Iberia and Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestries were found at the end of the Bell Beaker period (roughly 4000 bp). Brighter colours indicate a higher proportion of ancestry modelled. Values falling exactly on bin boundaries are included in the lower bin. Kriging was performed on the IBD mixture modelling set C4 results. The raw mixture modelling results for these ancestries can be visualized in Supplementary Fig. 1.33. Kriging results for roughly 4400 bp, 3300 bp and 2600 bp are also shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. b, IBD mixture modelling results for England, France and the Czech Republic during the Bronze and Iron Ages, highlighting the changes in southwestern and southeastern European Bronze Age-related ancestries from 4800 to 2000 bp. For each target individual (n = 602), point estimates of the proportions of ancestry modelled from these ancestry sources are plotted. For each point estimate, standard errors were calculated using a weighted block jackknife with n = 22 chromosomes, sequentially leaving out one chromosome at a time. The trendline shows the rolling median of the point estimates, using a window of 5. Base maps in a were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

Sampling is now relatively dense across the region of interest during much of the Bronze and Iron Age, with the exception of the cremation-dominated Urnfield Culture (3200–2800 bp). We therefore first focus on the well-sampled peripheries: England and the Czech Republic, where dense sampling continues throughout the Bronze and Iron Ages, and France, where Iron Age sampling has been greatly improved32. To visualize the changes through time, we plot the IBD mixture modelling proportions as timelines for England, France and the Czech Republic (Figs. 3b and 4b).

In England, the prominent Farmer ancestries change through time (Fig. 3b). Before 4000 bp, individuals tend to have a slightly higher proportion of local British–Irish Neo.-related ancestry relative to the other Neolithic-related ancestries. From 3800 bp to 3200 bp, Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry exceeds the local Neolithic ancestry (Fig. 3b), consistent with a “large-scale migration” from the mainland34,42. Between 3200 bp and 2800 bp, we see a shift, in which the proportion of Italy Neo.-related ancestry has increased to similar proportions to that of Iberia–France Neo.-related, coinciding with the appearance of Anatolia BA-related ancestry. Bronze Age sources (Fig. 4b) show S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry appearing in England between 4000 bp and 3200 bp, consistent with the appearance of Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry. Between 3200 bp and 2800 bp, we see Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry increasing, becoming widespread by at least 2600 bp (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 6).

In France, we see a similar transition (Fig. 3b). Before 3500 bp, more local Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry than Italy Neo.-related ancestry tends to be present. After 2800 bp, the relative proportions have reversed, so Italy Neo.-related ancestry is the highest, accompanied by Anatolia BA-related ancestry. When using the Bronze Age sources (Fig. 4b), we see an increase in the Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry and a decrease in the local S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry at corresponding times. However, because of the lack of samples from the Late Bronze Age, the time of this transition cannot be directly measured. Nevertheless, the increased proportions of Italy Neo.-related (set C3) and Hungary–Serbia BA-related (set C4) ancestry between 3200 bp and 2800 bp in Britain (Figs. 3, 4) and Iberia (Supplementary Fig. 1.35) suggests that this ancestry was present in France by this time. We also observe in France a subtle increase in East North Sea (ENS)-related ancestry between 2800–2470 bp and 2470–2000 bp, corresponding to the transition from Hallstatt to La Tène in France (Supplementary Fig. 1.46). ENS-related ancestry is found throughout the Bell Beaker region and is found in the highest proportions in the Netherlands throughout the Bronze and Iron Ages (Supplementary Fig. 1.10). Although limited sampling between the Netherlands, western Germany and northern France means that a more precise source region for this ancestry cannot be assessed, it should be noted that the transition occurs after the spread of Celtic under all models. Nevertheless, the subtle increase in ENS-related ancestry in France is consistent with the integration of more northern ancestry by the La Tène period, as suggested by previous studies35.

Further east, in the Czech Republic, an increase in Italy Neo.-related and Anatolia BA-related ancestry is observed by roughly 3300 bp in Tumulus-associated and Knovíz-associated individuals (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 3). Because Italy Neo.-related ancestry is also present east of the Adriatic Sea (Fig. 3a), this population movement need not originate in Italy. Consistent with the influence from the southeast inferred from the Neolithic ancestries, we detect an increase in Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry between 3600 bp and 3300 bp when including the Bronze Age sources (Fig. 4b). Unlike England, the Czech Republic shows no increase in Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry between 4000 bp and 2600 bp that would reflect a movement from western Europe (Fig. 3b). We do, however, note an increase in S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry from roughly 3300 bp (Fig. 4b). Combined, these results allow France and Iberia to be excluded as potential source regions from which the influx of ancestry came into the Czech Republic, and instead point to a movement from a region in which S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry is present yet Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry is absent, for example Italy (Supplementary Figs. 1.10 and 1.11) or central Europe (sets C3 and C4, Supplementary Fig. 1.37).

We interpret the persistent northwestern Bell Beaker-related ancestry together with shifts in local ancestry as resulting from several admixture processes between Bell Beaker-related populations and local Farmers across Europe, who subsequently moved within the region. Relative to the Celtic source regions proposed under linguistic models, we see movements to Britain from within the Celtic-from-the-West and Celtic-from-the-Centre source regions from 3800 bp, and from within the Celtic-from-the-East source regions from roughly 3200 bp.

The timing and distribution of the westward spread of Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry corresponds closely to the expansion of the Urnfield Culture (Supplementary Note 6). However, few genomes between 3200 bp and 2800 bp exist due to the Urnfield-associated practice of cremation. Including Urnfield context individuals from Iberia43 as IBD mixture modelling targets reveals an influx of Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry by 3150 bp (set C4, Supplementary Fig. 1.35), consistent with previous suggestions of an influx of ancestry from central Europe43,44. In the Czech Republic, individuals associated with the Urnfield subgroup of the Knovíz Culture are also represented in the dataset. Consistent with the results from the Urnfield context in Iberia, we find that the Knovíz individuals are modelled with high Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry (Extended Data Fig. 3). To test whether the Knovíz individuals represent Urnfield ancestry more broadly, we included Knovíz individuals as a source (set C5). By 2800 bp, when sampling improves, Knovíz-related ancestry is modelled in high proportions across western, southern and eastern central Europe in former Urnfield regions, complemented by more local sources (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8). We note that in this study, ‘Knovíz-related ancestry’ is used as a proxy for a broader group rather than representing people specifically of the Knovíz Culture.

In Iron Age England, the highest ancestry proportion tends to be modelled as Bell Beaker-related, followed by Knovíz-related and S. France–N. Iberia BA-related (Extended Data Fig. 7). By contrast, on the mainland, the proportion of ancestry modelled as Bell Beaker-related tends to be low or absent, with the Steppe ancestry in these individuals better modelled by the other Bronze Age sources, that is, Knovíz-related, S. France–N. Iberia BA-related and Hungary–Serbia BA-related. When including more Bronze Age sources from England (set C6) and France (set C7), the increase in Knovíz-related ancestry by roughly 2800 bp remains apparent (Supplementary Figs. 1.19 and 1.20). Thus, compared with England, the effect of Knovíz-related ancestry is particularly high in France, Germany and the Czech Republic (Extended Data Fig. 7). In Austria, we note considerable diversity at the eponymous Hallstatt archaeological site, with individuals modelled with particularly high proportions of either Knovíz-related or Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry, more similar to Hungary, Slovenia and Slovakia, where the Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry is modelled in high proportions (Extended Data Fig. 7). In Iberia, we see Knovíz-related ancestry becoming present in almost all individuals after 3200 bp (set C5, Supplementary Fig. 1.35). Although a number of individuals before this point are modelled with small proportions of Knovíz-related ancestry in set C5, they lack Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry (set C4, Supplementary Fig. 1.35) expected for movements from central Europe. The results here indicate gene flow from eastern central Europe occurring between 3200 bp and 2800 bp, coinciding with the expansion of the Urnfield Culture. We note that the genetic effects diminish the further west they spread. Finally, we note in the Czech Republic a subtle increase of S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry roughly 2400 bp, aligning with small proportions of Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry in set C3 (Supplementary Fig. 1.54), corresponding to the beginning of the La Tène period.

Identifying which populations were involved in the formation of the Knovíz-related ancestry profile remains difficult due to the lack of samples between 3700 bp and 3300 bp. Compared with the earlier Únětice individuals of the Czech Republic, we see that Knovíz-related individuals have experienced an influx of Italy Neo.-related ancestry (found around the Adriatic Sea roughly 4000 bp) and Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry (found in the Balkans roughly 4000 bp) (Extended Data Fig. 3), suggestive of an influence from the southeast. We also see a subtle increase in ENS-related ancestry, which is found across the entire Bell Beaker range but occurs in the highest proportions in the Netherlands, suggestive of influence from central or northwest Europe. As a result, the specific populations and time of formation remain unclear, as does the possibility of some degree of local genetic continuity. However, two signals are clear and relevant to this study. First, we do not see evidence of Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry in the Czech Republic from roughly 3300 bp to 2800 bp (Fig. 3b). The absence of this ancestry excludes western Europe as a potential source in the formation of Knovíz-related ancestry, which is of relevance to the evaluation of the Celtic-from-the-West and Celtic-from-the-Centre models. Second, we find that the Steppe ancestry in Knovíz individuals, as well as those across the entire Iron Age Celtic-speaking range, is modelled primarily as Bell Beaker-related rather than Corded Ware-related or extra Yamnaya-related ancestry (Fig. 2). In this historical period, Corded Ware-related ancestry is associated with Germanic-speaking populations in northern Europe32, and further Yamnaya-related ancestry (Supplementary Fig. 1.31b) with Greek-speaking populations in the Aegean33. Thus, regardless of the precise timing and populations involved in the formation of the Knovíz-related ancestry, its Steppe ancestry derives from Bell Beaker populations, suggesting that the dialect ancestral to Celtic, too, can ultimately be traced back to Bell Beaker groups. Improved sampling from Bronze Age northern Italy and central Europe will probably provide further insight into the formation of Knovíz-related ancestry (Supplementary Note 1), potentially also explaining the linguistic ties between the Celtic and Italic branches of the Indo-European language family (Supplementary Note 5).

We tested the robustness of these results using qpAdm, chromopainter and Y haplogroups. Full qpAdm results are provided in Supplementary Note 2, Supplementary Figs. 2.1 and 2.2 and Supplementary Tables 2.1–2.4, and full chromopainting results in Supplementary Note 3, Supplementary Figs. 3.1–3.7 and Supplementary Tables 3.1 and 3.2. Y chromosome analyses are provided in Supplementary Note 4. These independent analyses supported the main demographic events inferred through IBD mixture modelling: gene flow into Britain after the Bell Beaker period, and into western Europe from further east at the end of the Bronze Age.

Past population genetics is increasingly invoked to evaluate competing hypotheses in historical linguistics when language change is assumed to result from population movements and resulting admixtures11,12,16,17,32,33,34,35. Extending approaches from traditional archaeolinguistic syntheses45,46,47, the present study uses genetic evidence to assess which linguistic models require the fewest extra assumptions about population movement, timing and language persistence (Methods). We stress, however, that linguistic change is not exclusively driven by demographic factors and therefore does not necessarily leave behind a population genetic signature48,49.

With the above in mind, we set out to evaluate the four main linguistic models, based on different interpretations of historical-linguistic and archaeological data, for how Celtic could have acquired its historically documented range across the European continent. These are the Bell Beaker model; the Celtic-from-the-West model; the Celtic-from-the-Centre model and the Celtic-from-the-East model. Across the dataset, we identify three demographic processes that intersect differently with these four linguistic models (Fig. 5a,b): movement 1, the initial transmission of Steppe ancestry through the Bell Beaker region (4400–4000 bp); movement 2, population movements to Britain (3800–3200 bp) and movement 3, the westward spread of Knovíz-related ancestry from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp). We note that movements 1–3 are extended processes, not discrete single events.
